body: Swap your igblastn command for alignair predict, keep reading the same AIRR table, and learn the few columns that differ.

The model carries its germline set, so there is nothing to build. The first run downloads the model and caches it. title: Your germline database
body: IgBLAST searches the databases you build. An AlignAIR model calls from the germline set it was trained with: OGRDB sets for the human IG models, IMGT sets for the TCR models. Choose a model lists each model's set and allele counts.

title: Allele names on the IG models
body: The IG models call alleles by their OGRDB labels. IGH V alleles read IGHVF10-G50*02 (F for the family, G for the gene group), where IgBLAST with IMGT germlines writes names such as IGHV3-23*01. IGH D and J alleles keep IMGT-style names (IGHD3-10*01, IGHJ6*02). IGK and IGL alleles have OGRDB labels of their own, such as IGKV1-5TCS*03 and IGLJ2/3-HDWH*01. The TCR models use IMGT names. So a join on v_call with an IgBLAST table, a gene-usage plot, or a genotype file in IMGT names will not match the IG models' calls. Two ways through: Bind IMGT's germline set with --reference: the calls then carry IMGT names ( Call with IMGT's set). Map the model's labels to IMGT names by their sequences, and translate your tables or AlignAIR's calls ( Map the labels to IMGT names).

title: Bind another germline set
body: Give a FASTA of V, D and J alleles whose headers are the allele names (>IGHV3-23*01), or IMGT/GENE-DB headers, which are read as they are (the field with a * names the allele). Novel alleles are welcome. Missing IMGT gaps and anchors are taken from the model's own alleles where it can. Nothing is retrained. The FASTA must hold every segment the model calls (the IGH model refuses one without D alleles), and keep to the model's locus: one that mixes in alleles of another locus is refused. The details are on Use your own germline reference.

title: Column by column
body: The shared AIRR columns keep their meaning. These are the ones to know: sequence_id, sequence, locus, rev_comp, productive, vj_in_frame, stop_codon, junction, junction_aa, junction_length, np1, np2 , <> The same in both. The T/F columns are the strings T and F: in pandas, compare with == "T". , ], [ <>v_sequence_start to j_germline_end, <> 1-based positions in the read and in the germline allele. AlignAIR's v_germline_start and v_germline_end count in the IMGT-gapped V germline from its first position, as Change-O's MakeDb writes them (so v_germline_start is 1); IgBLAST's count in the ungapped allele. , ], [ <>v_call, d_call, j_call, <> v_call lists the V alleles that match the read equally well, comma-separated after the call (read02 below); AlignAIR's d_call and j_call name one allele. On the IG models the names are OGRDB labels. , ], [ <>v_identity, d_identity, j_identity, <> AlignAIR writes a fraction from 0 to 1, as the AIRR standard defines it; IgBLAST writes a percentage. A filter "v_identity >= 98" becomes "v_identity >= 0.98". , ], [ <>sequence_alignment, germline_alignment, "AlignAIR's are IMGT-gapped (dots in the V gaps), the form Change-O works with.", ], [ <>v_cigar, d_cigar, j_cigar, <> Both span the whole read: S for the read's bases outside the segment, N for the germline bases skipped at its start, then the alignment (4N291M73S). IgBLAST's also ends with an N for the germline bases after the segment, which the AIRR standard leaves optional. , ], [ <>fwr1 to fwr4, cdr1 to cdr3, with their starts and ends, <> The positions are the same: 1-based, in the read. How far to trust the calls explains both. , ], [ c_call, <> AlignAIR does not call the constant region: the column stays blank unless a --metadata table fills it (Cell Ranger's c_gene). , ], ] /> A real row (read02 of the example reads), where two V alleles match the read equally well:

title: Columns only AlignAIR writes
body: Two habits to add to an IgBLAST pipeline: Keep the rows with airr_assembly_status complete before junction-level work. A partial row has valid calls but some fields left blank; airr_assembly_reason says why. Read a *_call_set with several alleles as "not resolved to one allele". It is the model's set before the germline refinement, so the call can fall outside it. Every column, with its unit and the presets that include it, is in the output column dictionary.

title: A fair side-by-side
body: To compare the two tools, give IgBLAST the germline set the model calls from, so both choose among the same alleles. The steps for the IGH model: reference export reads a model file: alignair models path prints where the model's file is (downloading it first if needed). The awk line reads the fifth character of each header, the segment letter after the three-letter locus (the same for IGK, IGL and the TCR loci).

title: The auxiliary J file
body: IgBLAST finds each J allele's reading frame and CDR3 end in its auxiliary file, by allele name. A J allele the file does not list gets no junction. This lists the J alleles it lacks: IGDATA is IgBLAST's own directory, where igblastn also finds its internal data. For the IGH model, the release's human_gl.aux should cover the J alleles. The IGK and IGL models' J alleles have OGRDB labels (IGKJ2-27FL*01) it does not list: copy the file and add one line per missing allele, in its tab-separated format: the allele name, the first coding frame start, the chain type ( JK or JL), the CDR3 end and the extra bases after the last codon, positions counted from 0.

title: Run both, then compare
body: For a locus without D (IGK, IGL, TRA, TRG), igblastn still asks for a D database: a one-sequence placeholder is enough, as it searches no D on those chains. Use -ig_seqtype TCR for the TCR models. The report gives, per gene, how often the two tools call the same allele and the same gene, and the set rescue: of the reads where the calls differ, how often IgBLAST's call is inside AlignAIR's *_call_set (shared ambiguity rather than a conflict). Agreement is not accuracy: without known truth, neither tool is the reference. The measured comparison, on simulated reads with known truth for all seven loci, is on Comparison with IgBLAST.

title: Coming from MiXCR
body: What AlignAIR takes over from a MiXCR pipeline (assigning V(D)J alleles to reads), what it leaves to other tools, and how to give it your reads.

title: Two different jobs
body: MiXCR covers the whole road from raw sequencing data to clonotypes. It aligns reads to V, D, J and C genes, corrects UMI and cell barcodes, assembles clonotypes and contigs, and exports clone tables and QC reports, usually through one mixcr analyze command with a preset for the library. AlignAIR does one step of that road: it assigns V, D and J alleles to each read, from a named germline set, and writes an AIRR rearrangement table with one row per read. It does not assemble clones.

title: What maps and what does not
body: alignair predict: allele calls with their ties, the junction, IMGT-gapped alignments, FWR and CDR regions. , ], [ "Its built-in gene library", <> The model's germline set (OGRDB for the IG models, IMGT for the TCR models), or your own with --reference. Allele names differ between the two tools. , ], ["Several loci in one run", "One model per locus: give each model the reads of its locus."], [ "C gene alignment (isotypes)", <> Not called. c_call comes only from a --metadata table, such as Cell Ranger's c_gene. , ], ["Paired-end FASTQ files", "One sequence per read: merge the pairs first."], [ "UMI and cell-barcode correction", <> None. Build one consensus read per UMI first (below), and carry barcodes and counts in with --metadata. , ], [ "Clonotype and contig assembly", <> None: AlignAIR does not assemble contigs, pair chains or group reads into clonotypes. For T cells, see T-cell clonotypes; for B cells, Change-O or SCOPer ( how). , ], [ "Clone tables and QC reports", <> The per-read AIRR table; alignair analyze prints a summary of it. , ], ["Receptor reads found in bulk RNA-seq", "Not covered: AlignAIR expects reads that are receptor sequences."], ] /> Keep MiXCR when you want its end-to-end pipeline to clonotypes. Reach for AlignAIR when the allele calls themselves feed your analysis: donor genotypes (--genotype, --infer-genotype), novel alleles (--reference), and the Immcantation tools that work from them.

title: Where AlignAIR fits
body: Prepare the reads. Merge read pairs, and for UMI libraries build one consensus read per UMI ( below). Cell Ranger's contigs need neither: align them as they are. Assign alleles. alignair predict with the model of each locus. Group clonotypes. T cells: by V gene, J gene and junction, with no threshold ( below). B cells, which hypermutate: Change-O's DefineClones.py or SCOPer, with a distance threshold ( Coming from Immcantation). Go on downstream. T cells: Scirpy and other tools that read AIRR tables ( below). B cells: germlines, genotypes, mutation and lineage analysis with the rest of Immcantation.

title: Merged reads
body: AlignAIR turns each read the right way round itself (the orientation and rev_comp columns say how), so reads in mixed orientations are fine. IUPAC ambiguity codes are read as N; a read in which more than 20% of the symbols are something else (a gap, a digit) is dropped, and --rejects-out keeps the dropped reads in a file. A read longer than 575 nt is aligned on its first 575 nt only (length_cropped is T). The cut comes before the read is turned: a forward read loses its 3' end, a reverse-complemented one the start of its V. A row cut inside its J is partial (j_cropped). Trim long reads to the V(D)J region first. Cell Ranger's contigs are forward, and the cut usually takes only constant region after the J. See Prepare your input.

title: UMI consensus reads and their counts
body: AlignAIR aligns each read as it is. It does not group reads by UMI, correct UMI or barcode errors, or build a consensus, so two reads of one molecule get two rows. Build the consensus reads first: MiXCR builds its own inside its pipeline, and AlignAIR needs them as sequences (FASTA, FASTQ or a table). Outside MiXCR, pRESTO's BuildConsensus.py builds one read per UMI from reads whose UMI is in their header ( pRESTO's documentation has workflows for UMI libraries); pRESTO is installed with Change-O. Then align the consensus reads, and join their counts by read id with --metadata. A table with a sequence_id column and columns such as umi_count, consensus_count, duplicate_count or sample_id adds them to each row: By default the join carries the known AIRR and 10x columns it finds; --keep-columns picks them yourself. Join sample and cell metadata has the rules.

title: 10x single-cell contigs
body: Cell Ranger's barcode, umis, reads and c_gene become cell_id, umi_count, consensus_count and c_call. A contig file holds every chain, and each model calls one locus, so split the contigs by the annotations' chain column first and align each chain with its own model: a TRA contig given to the TRB model can come out as a complete, productive TRB row. Join sample and cell metadata gives the split, for TRA, TRB, TRG and TRD alike, and how to put the tables back together.

title: T-cell clonotypes
body: T cells do not hypermutate, so a T-cell clonotype is usually the reads, or cells, with the same V gene, J gene and junction, base for base or in amino acids. No distance threshold is chosen, unlike the SHazaM threshold of B-cell clones. Change-O's DefineClones.py groups them with a distance of 0: It writes TRB_clone-pass.tsv with a clone_id column. A row without a junction cannot be grouped, and DefineClones counts it as failed. For single cells, a clonotype usually also pairs the chains of each cell (by cell_id): Scirpy does that, below.

title: Scirpy and other tools
body: Scirpy reads AlignAIR's tables as they are, one per locus, and puts the chains with the same cell_id together (the cell_id comes from Cell Ranger's annotations, through --metadata). Checked with Scirpy 0.26.1, on the TRA and TRB tables of 300 simulated cells: define_clonotypes groups the cells whose chains have the same CDR3 in nucleotides; same_v_gene=True also asks for the same V gene. index_chains keeps the productive chains of each cell. Other tools that read the AIRR rearrangement format take AlignAIR's table the same way; check the columns each one needs.

title: Check the calls against Cell Ranger or MiXCR
body: alignair compare matches two AIRR tables row by row on sequence_id and reports, per segment, how often the calls agree. Cell Ranger's airr_rearrangement.tsv names each row by its contig id, as in filtered_contig.fasta, so it matches AlignAIR's table of the same contigs as it is (the rows of the other chains count as Cell Ranger's only). A MiXCR table matches only when its sequence_id holds your read ids. On 300 simulated TRB contigs, against a table in Cell Ranger's layout that names each contig's true genes, without alleles: Read the gene agreement column. A table that names genes only, or alleles of another germline set (Cell Ranger's reference, MiXCR's library), agrees on no allele name, so its allele agreement says nothing. Where the tools differ, either may be right. Evaluate your model explains the rest of the report.

title: What has been measured on T-cell receptors
body: The comparison with IgBLAST measures the four TCR models, like the IG models, on simulated reads with known truth. Its check on real reads covers human IGH repertoires only, whose donors' alleles are known from their genomes; no real TCR repertoire has been scored that way. So judge the TCR models by the simulated results, and check a sample of your own reads against the tool you use today, as above.

title: Coming from Immcantation
body: Replace AssignGenes and MakeDb with one alignair predict, and keep Change-O, TIgGER and SCOPer on the table it writes.

title: AssignGenes and MakeDb become one command
body: In the usual Change-O route, AssignGenes.py igblast runs IgBLAST on the reads, and MakeDb.py igblast turns IgBLAST's output into an AIRR table with IMGT-gapped alignments. AlignAIR does both in one step: its table is already AIRR, with an IMGT-gapped sequence_alignment and germline_alignment. Keep the default columns (all 99). Change-O, TIgGER and SCOPer read sequence_alignment, junction_length and locus, and the lighter presets (core, airr, minimal) each drop some of them. When a read cannot tell V alleles apart, v_call lists the call and then the alleles that match the read as well, comma-separated, as IgBLAST does. Change-O and TIgGER read these lists as they read IgBLAST's. Reads from pRESTO keep their whole header as sequence_id: AlignAIR does not split >read01|CONSCOUNT=2|DUPCOUNT=5|PRCONS=IGHG into the consensus_count and duplicate_count columns MakeDb writes. Prepare your input shows how to cut the headers to the read id and join the annotations back with --metadata.

title: Germlines for CreateGermlines
body: CreateGermlines.py rebuilds each read's germline from IMGT-gapped V alleles named as in the table. Export them from the model: --gapped writes each V allele IMGT-gapped and D and J as they are, all in one FASTA, under the names the model calls. reference export reads a model file: alignair models path prints where the model's file is (downloading it first if needed). Then build the germlines from AlignAIR's table as it is: Where the AIRR schema leaves a choice, AlignAIR's table counts as MakeDb does, so CreateGermlines reads it unchanged. v_germline_start and v_germline_end are positions in the IMGT-gapped V germline, from its first position, as sequence_alignment lays out the V. The untemplated bases are N in germline_alignment. A row without a D call holds every base between V and J in np1. The CIGARs count ungapped germline bases, as the schema says. CreateGermlines writes alignair_germ-pass.tsv with a germline_alignment_d_mask column, the germline Change-O's later steps read. Its log counts the rows it could not build; Change-O's --failed option writes them to a file. Most of those are partial rows ( airr_assembly_status), which have no gapped alignment. A complete row also fails when its J alignment has more or fewer germline bases than read bases (an insertion or deletion in J). CreateGermlines takes the J's length from j_germline_start and j_germline_end, while sequence_alignment keeps the read's own J bases. On 3,000 real IGH reads, 2,855 of the 2,872 complete rows passed; each of the other 17 has such a J. With novel alleles, give CreateGermlines the FASTA you bound with --reference, the export with the novel alleles added (TIgGER on AlignAIR's table).

title: Donor genotypes
body: TIgGER infers a donor's V genotype from a table, and can re-assign each read's alleles to that genotype. AlignAIR's --genotype does the re-assignment inside the alignment: given the donor's alleles, it calls only from them. The file is YAML or JSON keyed by segment, "V: [...], D: [...], J: [...]": The V list is the donor's whole V genotype: V alleles it does not list are not called. A segment it leaves out (here D and J) keeps all its alleles.

title: IMGT names and OGRDB names
body: A genotype must name alleles the way the model does. A genotype made from IgBLAST calls against IMGT germlines names alleles such as IGHV3-23*01. The IG models call OGRDB labels, so AlignAIR refuses it: Three ways through: Make the genotype from AlignAIR's own calls. Use alignair genotype or --infer-genotype (below), or run TIgGER on AlignAIR's table ( how): the names are then the model's. Translate the names. Match the model's alleles to IMGT names by sequence, then write the model's labels into the genotype (Map the labels to IMGT names ). Keep IMGT names. Bind IMGT's germline set with --reference; Immcantation's IMGT/GENE-DB files are read as they are, headers included. The calls then carry IMGT names, and the IMGT genotype fits (Call with IMGT's set). The TCR models call IMGT names, so an IMGT-named genotype fits them as it is.

title: alignair genotype: a genotype from any table
body: alignair genotype reads any tool's AIRR table and infers the V genotype. For each V gene it keeps the most frequent alleles among the rows whose v_call is a single allele, until they explain 87.5% of those rows (--explain), the share TIgGER's inferGenotype also uses. It differs from inferGenotype in two ways: it counts every such row, mutated or not, where inferGenotype counts only unmutated reads by default (find_unmutated = TRUE); a gene with fewer than 10 such rows (--min-reads) has too little evidence and is left open, a cutoff of AlignAIR's own. It writes an AIRR GenotypeSet; --locus names its locus (default IGH). On 29,101 reads of one donor (the first 30,000 read pairs of ENA run SRR8283604, merged): A gene is left open when few of its rows name a single allele, however many rows it has: 4,367 of the 4,371 reads called to IGHVF10-G41 here list *02 and *03 together, as they start after the bases that tell the two apart. The GenotypeSet goes straight back into --genotype: A GenotypeSet restricts only the genes it names. A gene it left open keeps all its alleles: in the run above, the 4,388 reads of the six open genes all kept their gene. --infer-genotype does both steps in one run. It reads the input twice: once to call, once to re-call the reads whose call the genotype excludes while they tie an allele it allows. A gene with fewer than --genotype-min-reads single-allele reads keeps every allele. The genotype goes to alignair.tsv.genotype.json (--genotype-out). More on Align with a donor genotype.

title: TIgGER on AlignAIR's table
body: TIgGER reads AlignAIR's table as it reads MakeDb's: v_call, j_call, the IMGT-gapped sequence_alignment, junction and junction_length. Its germline file is the --gapped export (above): IMGT-gapped V alleles, named as the table names them. Keep that one file for the whole round trip: TIgGER reads it, the novel alleles TIgGER finds are added to it, and AlignAIR and CreateGermlines both read the result.

title: Novel alleles and the genotype
body: On the 29,101 reads above, selectNovel(novel) holds two novel alleles of IGHVF6-G21, named the TIgGER way (the allele they differ from, then each substitution at its IMGT position): IGHVF6-G21*12_G163A and IGHVF6-G21*16_G54A. The genotype keeps the first. These reads start near IMGT position 40, and their first few bases differ from every germline, as a primer's do: with the default pos_range (1 to 312), findNovelAlleles also reported "novel" alleles of four genes at positions 42 to 46. Leave out the positions your primers cover.

title: Back into AlignAIR
body: AlignAIR does not read TIgGER's genotype table: written to a TSV and given to --genotype, it is refused: In the same R session, write the genotype as a YAML genotype, and the novel alleles' gapped sequences (TIgGER's novel_imgt) after the gapped germlines: Then align with both, and build the germlines from the same file: 840 of the 29,101 reads are now called to the novel allele (the fifth column is v_call). A YAML genotype calls only the V alleles it lists, as TIgGER's reassignAlleles does: the reads of a gene TIgGER left out of the genotype move to another gene or lose their V call (492 reads here). To keep such genes whole, use alignair genotype's GenotypeSet instead ( above). The novel alleles carry the model's labels, as the table does. To work in IMGT names throughout, bind IMGT's gapped germline set (Call with IMGT's set) and use that file where these steps use germlines.fasta: TIgGER and CreateGermlines read its IMGT/GENE-DB headers too. On the same reads, with IMGT's human IGH set bound, TIgGER found the same novel allele as IGHV1-69*04_G54A, and 840 reads were called to it. To translate labels instead, see Map the labels to IMGT names.

title: v_call_genotyped
body: TIgGER's reassignAlleles writes its genotyped calls to a new column, v_call_genotyped, and the steps after it are pointed at that column (DefineClones.py --vf v_call_genotyped, for example). A --genotype run needs no such step: its v_call already holds calls from the donor's alleles, and AlignAIR writes no v_call_genotyped column. Point those steps at v_call, or run reassignAlleles on AlignAIR's table if your pipeline expects the column: it reads the table as it is.

title: TIgGER, alignair genotype or --infer-genotype?
body: TIgGER's findNovelAlleles. AlignAIR finds none: it calls only alleles of the germline set it runs with. , ], [ "A genotype from unmutated reads only, as in a heavily mutated repertoire", <> TIgGER's inferGenotype (unmutated reads by default), or its Bayesian form, inferGenotypeBayesian. , ], [ "A genotype without R, from any tool's AIRR table, that leaves genes with little evidence open", <> alignair genotype, then --genotype genotype.json. , ], [ "The genotype applied in the same run, settling the reads whose v_call ties an allele of the genotype with others", --infer-genotype, ], ] />

title: Clonal clustering: Change-O and SCOPer
body: Change-O's clonal clustering runs on the table from CreateGermlines: --act set groups reads by every gene of a tied call, so AlignAIR's comma-separated calls are used whole. The threshold 0.16 is only an example: choose yours from your data's distance-to-nearest distribution (SHazaM). The result, alignair_germ-pass_clone-pass.tsv, adds a clone_id column. T cells need no threshold (T-cell clonotypes). SCOPer reads the same table in R. Its clone functions group rows by v_call and j_call and compare junction, the column names AlignAIR writes. For single-cell data they also use cell_id, which --metadata carries from Cell Ranger's barcodes ( Join sample and cell metadata).

title: nf-core/airrflow
body: airrflow takes AlignAIR's table in its assembled mode. By default it re-assigns genes in an AIRR table it is given, which would replace AlignAIR's calls: run it with --reassign false. Its samplesheet needs more columns than the file name (sample, subject, species, locus and others): take the list from airrflow's usage docs for the version you run. airrflow then builds germlines and clones with Change-O and SCOPer from its own germline reference: give it AlignAIR's table as it is (CreateGermlines reads it, above), and a reference whose allele names match the table's (OGRDB labels for the IG models). Its parameter docs say how to give it one.

title: From a read to an AIRR row
body: alignair predict and the Python API run the same path. cli/predict.py adds the file handling around it: streaming, the metadata join, the genotype pass and the run record.

title: 1. Load the model
body: Aligner.from_pretrained turns the model spec into a local file with registry.resolve_model: a path is used as it is; a catalog id or id@version is looked up in the registries and downloaded once into the cache, checked against the catalog's SHA-256; hf://org/repo comes from that Hugging Face repo. model_file.load_model then restores the weights (AlignAIR.from_state_dict, strict on names and shapes), takes the reference from the file's reference_json section, or the --reference FASTA annotated against it, and binds it ( bind_reference), which compiles the bank. A genotype binds a subset of that reference ( Aligner.with_genotype, genotype_bank): the bank keeps only its rows.

title: 2. Read the input
body: io.iter_sequence_batches streams the input in chunks (--chunk-size, 20,000 reads). It uppercases each read, turns IUPAC ambiguity codes into N, drops a read with more than 20% other symbols, and renames a repeated id _dup1, _dup2. With --metadata, io.build_metadata_index indexes the table in a temporary SQLite file, and each chunk's rows are looked up by read id.

title: 3. Run the pipeline
body: Each chunk goes to Aligner.predict, or, with --threads N, to parallel.ProcessPool, whose single-threaded workers each hold a copy of the aligner. Aligner.predict builds a PredictConfig and calls predict.predict, which runs PIPELINE: twelve stages, each a function of predict/stages.py that takes a PredictionState and returns a copy with its own fields set. input_policy, prepare_reads, <>reads, cropped, "Cuts each read to the model's window (575 nt) and flags the cut ones."], [forward, run_forward, batches, <>The forward pass, batch by batch; each batch's outputs typed as ModelOutputs.], [clean, decode_outputs, predictions, "Merges the batches; a boundary is the argmax of its position logits."], [canonicalize, canonicalize_reads, canonical, "Turns each read to its forward orientation."], [segments, correct_spans, segments, "Integer V, D and J spans, inside the read and in order."], [alleles, select_calls, calls, "Each gene's candidate set from the allele scores."], [germline, align_reads, alignments, "Places each call in its germline: read and germline coordinates, CIGAR."], [better_v, promote_better_v, alignments, "A bound V allele the read matches better than the call becomes the call (how a novel allele is called)."], [v_presence, find_absent_v, no_v, "Finds the reads that hold no V."], [ties, list_v_ties, v_ties, "Lists the V alleles the read cannot tell from its call."], [records, build_records, results, <>Each read's typed result (ReadResult).], [airr, build_rows, rows, <>The AIRR rows (predict.airr.build_airr): junction and productivity from the anchors, IMGT-gapped alignments, regions, identities, flags.], ] />

title: Inside the forward stage
body: predict.forward.run_model batches reads of similar width (bucket_batches), runs the model in evaluation mode and refuses a non-finite output. On one batch, AlignAIR.forward does: predict.outputs.ModelOutputs.from_network is the one place the pipeline reads the model's output keys: a missing required key or an unknown one is an InferenceError.

title: 4. Write the table

The column presets are io.airr.COLUMN_PRESETS. cli/predict.py then writes <out>.run.json: the model, the bound reference's digests, the options and the read counts.

title: Training
body: run_training(config) (train/workflow.py) is the one entry point. alignair train builds a TrainingConfig, calls it, and exports a bundle. In order: Reference. The config's dataconfigs (GenAIRR's built-in germline sets, or one built from FASTA files) resolve through alignair.genairr into a ReferenceSet. Model. prepare_model(reference, ..., **config.model_options).build_model(). With init_from, train.transfer.transfer_compatible_weights copies every tensor whose name and shape match; the rest start fresh. Objective. tasks.build_tasks(config) asks the architecture for its objective ( ChipObjective for the chip). Reads. train.records.training_records draws GenAIRR records from the curriculum's streams (CurriculumStreamPolicy), each stream from its own block of seeds ( train.records.seeds.seed_block); part of them come from synthetic novel V alleles ( NovelAlleles), many with library flanks (data.flanks.FlankPolicy). With data_workers above 0 the streams run in worker processes (train/records/workers.py, train/assembly.py) and give the same batches as one process does. Batches. data.adapters.NucleotideBatchAdapter turns records into tensors and the chip's per-base targets (data/chip_inputs.py), each read in one of the four orientations. Steps. The engine (train/setup.py, train/engine.py) runs AdamW updates, with an optional cosine learning-rate schedule (CosineSchedule); train/guards.py stops a run on a non-finite loss or gradient. A run's on_iteration callback sees each step. Checkpoints. train/checkpoints.py saves rotating checkpoints and the best one with model_file.save_model, pickle sections included, so a run resumes (resume_path). train.bundle.export_bundle (alignair export) writes the pickle-free model to share. The user's side of this is on Train a model for your reference and Fine-tune a model.

title: The model file
body: One .alignair file per model holds everything a run needs: the weights, the configuration and the germline reference. Its byte layout (), integers little-endian: b"ALGNAIR", the format tag], ["7", "1", <>The major format version (MAJOR_VERSION, 1); a reader refuses a newer one.], ["8", "8", <>u64: H, the JSON header's length in bytes], ["16", H, "The JSON header, UTF-8"], [<>16 + H, "...", "The sections' blobs, back to back, each compressed on its own"], ] /> The header's sections maps each section's name to its blob: offset (counted from the end of the header), compressed_length, payload_length, codec ( none, zlib or zstd; reading zstd needs the zstandard package), compressed_sha256 and payload_sha256 (both checked on every read), and format (json, safetensors, fasta, python-pickle or bytes). Its other keys describe the model ( model_file.io.save_model writes them): the format versions, the model's settings, its training, its reference's digests (allele_order_sha256, reference_fasta_sha256), its provenance and the card's descriptive fields (model_id, model_version, description, license). config, "JSON", "portable", <>The AlignAIRConfig: architecture name, widths, window.], [weights, "safetensors", "portable", "The weights."], [reference, "FASTA", "portable", "The reference's alleles."], [reference_json, "JSON", "portable", "The full reference (anchors, gapped forms, loci); a model loads its reference from it."], [dataconfig/<i>, "pickle", "trusted", "Each GenAIRR dataconfig the model trained on."], [train_state, "pickle", "trusted", "The optimizer, scheduler and random state."], ] /> A file is one of two kinds. body: The model always embeds the read and corrects its orientation; everything after that is the architecture's core. The model calls it as core(emb, mask, end_mask, *, tokens, batch) with the corrected embedding, the read and end masks, the corrected tokens and the raw batch, and adds the dict it returns to its outputs. title: Pipeline hooks
body: run_stages(state, stages=PIPELINE, hooks=()) wraps every stage call in each hook, hook(stage, state, run), the first hook outermost; a hook may replace what a stage returns. A run of fewer stages (PIPELINE[:3]) stops early. A stage that leaves a field it sets unset is an InferenceError.

title: Another source of training reads
body: run_training(config, record_source=...) replaces the GenAIRR provider of every training and validation stream. A RecordSource is a callable (dataconfig, parameters, seed) that returns fresh record mappings; with data_workers above 0 it runs in worker processes, so it must pickle.

title: Registries
body: A model id is looked up in the registries, in this order: --registry (or registry=), then ALIGNAIR_REGISTRY (comma-separated), then the registries list of config.toml in AlignAIR's config directory (~/.config/alignair on Linux; the config_dir line of alignair doctor), then the shared catalog. A registry is hf://org/repo, an https:// URL, or a file:// path: any directory that holds a registry.json and its model files. Publishing to the catalog has the format.

title: What to build on
body: The supported API is what alignair, alignair.io, alignair.genotype, alignair.registry, alignair.reference and alignair.train export ( Python API), with the extension points above. The training engine and loop ( train.engine, train.loop) and the modules whose names start with an underscore are internal and change without notice.

title: Release claims and the public models
body: tests.support.claims.CLAIM_TESTS maps each release claim of the model card to the test that proves it. The model-acceptance workflow (.github/workflows/model-validation.yml) fetches the models that tests/fixtures/models/validation.json pins, through AlignAIR's verified downloader, then requires every claim's test to pass: The tests read the cache offline, after rechecking each file's size and checksum; they never fall back to another model. These are regression checks on simulated reads; the accuracy claims come from the comparison with IgBLAST.

title: Writing a test
body: Use deterministic inputs and assert what can be observed: values, shapes, coordinates, a saved file's contents, or the error class and code a bad input raises. Go through public entry points where you can. Declare the layer. Keep small fixtures beside their tests and shared ones in the nearest conftest.py; import helpers from tests/support, not from another test module. The root fixture repo_root is the repository's path; write outputs to tmp_path. Each test gets its own AlignAIR, XDG and Hugging Face cache and config directories, and a random seed derived from its node id; Python's, NumPy's and PyTorch's random state, the default dtype, gradient mode, deterministic settings and the thread count are restored afterwards. Torch runs on 2 threads. A connection or DNS lookup outside the machine fails the test (loopback works). Inject a provider's response instead of fetching it. When you move a test that a release claim names, update tests.support.claims.CLAIM_TESTS.

Never edit them by hand. From the repository root, with AlignAIR importable: It writes cli-options.json, output-columns.json, error-codes.json, python-api.json and search-index.json. Run it after you change a CLI option or its help, an output column or its description (io/columns_doc.py), an error class, a public signature or docstring, or a docs page's title or headings (the search index lists them); then commit the changed files with your change. Two files need inputs from outside the code: comparison.json takes only the reports of a locked test-split run of the comparison harness; a development-split report is refused.

title: The catalog
body: The pretrained models live in one public Hugging Face repo, AlignAIR/AlignAIR-pretrained (DEFAULT_REGISTRY, hf://AlignAIR/AlignAIR-pretrained). It holds a catalog, registry.json, and for each version of each model three files: the pickle-free <id>/<version>.alignair, its .model_card.md and its .reference_manifest.json. --model alignair4-igh-human and Aligner.from_pretrained("alignair4-igh-human") read it. Anyone reads it, with no account: alignair models list and --model <id> download anonymously. Only maintainers write it, with a Hugging Face write token. No alignair command writes to it; the Python calls below do. No code change is needed for a new version. AlignAIR reads registry.json when it looks a model up: once a new version is uploaded, alignair models list shows it, a run on the plain id downloads it, and alignair models update fetches it for the models already in a cache.

title: 1. Export the bundle
body: alignair export turns a training checkpoint into a bundle: the pickle-free model.alignair, model_card.md, reference_manifest.json and, unless --no-validate, validation_report.json (scores on a fixed held-out stream). The id and version go into the model file's card, where the catalog checks them. Never publish a training checkpoint; the catalog refuses one. Export from an installed AlignAIR release: the card records the version that wrote it in created_by_alignair, which is 0+unknown from a source tree that is not installed. A bundle exported without an id or version can be carded afterwards with alignair.model_file.update_card(src, dst, """model_id": ..., "model_version": ...""), which changes descriptive header fields only and carries every section over byte for byte.

title: 2. Add it to a local copy of the catalog
body: Start from a full copy of the hub's catalog: publish_bundle validates every version the local registry.json lists, and the upload replaces the hub's registry.json with yours. publish_bundle lays the bundle out as the catalog serves it ( alignair4-igh-human/1.0.0.alignair with its card and manifest beside it), adds the version to registry.json with every checksum, and makes the version latest when it is the highest. It is transactional: it stages the files, validates the catalog as it would be, and only then moves the files and the new registry.json into place. On a problem it returns the list and writes nothing. Before uploading, load it from the local copy as a user would:

title: 3. Upload the version
body: upload_version validates the version again (ModelNotFoundError when the local catalog lacks it, RegistryInvalidError when it fails a check), then sends its three files and registry.json in one commit, so the hub never lists a version without its files. It needs huggingface_hub (pip install "alignair[hub]"). Then check as an anonymous user, on another machine or with a fresh ALIGNAIR_CACHE_DIR:

title: What is checked
body: validate_registry(catalog, artifact_path) () is the gate: publish_local, publish_bundle and upload_version all run it. For every version of every model it checks that: the model file exists, and its size and SHA-256 are the catalog's; it has no pickle section (no dataconfig/*, no train_state) and has a reference_json; both reference digests recompute from that reference_json, and equal the catalog's; its card has model_id, model_version, model_format_version and created_by_alignair, and its id and version are the catalog's; each companion file exists with the catalog's SHA-256; latest names a listed version. It returns a list of problems, empty when all pass. To check a whole catalog directory: On the user's side, alignair models verify [MODEL] re-hashes the models in the cache against the registry and prints OK, MISMATCH or UNKNOWN (not in registry) for each; it exits with 1 on a mismatch.

title: Start with an issue
body: Open an issue first for a change that is more than a small fix, so the approach is agreed before you write it. The issue templates are a bug report, a feature request, and a model or reference request (a species or locus you would like a pretrained model for, or a germline set that fails to parse or train). For a bug, include alignair doctor --json, the command, and, for a prediction problem, a small input file; the --debug traceback and the <out>.run.json beside the table help too. Report a security problem privately, as says, not in an issue.

title: Branch, test, open a pull request
body: Work on a branch of your fork, and open the pull request against main. Keep it focused on one change, and match the surrounding style; no large unrelated reformatting. Add tests for new behaviour, each declaring its layer (component, integration or acceptance) and writing its outputs to tmp_path. python -m pytest must pass, and so must ruff check src/alignair. When users see the change, update the docs and CHANGELOG.md; when a CLI option, column, error or public docstring changes, regenerate the site's data (python website/scripts/site_data.py). The pull request template has a checklist of the same. On every pull request, CI runs the suite on Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12 with coverage, the component tests in a shuffled order and in parallel workers, platform tests on Linux, macOS and Windows, a built wheel through the release smoke test, the conda recipe and the model-acceptance tests; the website's build and tests run when website/ changes.

title: Contributing

title: Changelog
body: What AlignAIR 4 brings, in short; every change is in the changelog on GitHub.

title: Models
body: Seven pretrained human models, one per locus: IGH, IGK, IGL, TRA, TRB, TRD and TRG. They download by id on first use and are cached (Choose a model). A model file is self-contained: the weights, the germline set and a card, loaded without running any code. alignair info prints a model's card.

title: Germline sets and genotypes
body: A model calls from the germline set it is given. --reference germline.fasta binds your own set, novel alleles and new genes included, with no training; missing IMGT gaps and anchors are filled from the model's own alleles (Use your own germline reference). --genotype limits the calls to a donor's alleles; --infer-genotype infers the donor's V genotype from the reads in the same run, by TIgGER's frequency rule; alignair genotype writes one from any AIRR table as an AIRR GenotypeSet (Align with a donor genotype). alignair reference export --gapped writes a model's germline set with IMGT-gapped V alleles, as Change-O's CreateGermlines.py needs.

title: Calls and output
body: v_call lists, after the call, the alleles that match the read equally well, as IgBLAST does; an allele of the germline set that matches the read at more bases than the model's call becomes the call. The junction and productivity follow by rule from the V Cys and J Trp/Phe codons found in the read. The output is an AIRR rearrangement table (99 columns, or a preset with --columns), with a .run.json record of the model, germline set and options beside it ( Output columns explained).

title: Running
body: --threads N aligns on the CPU in N worker processes; the batch size follows the device ( Run at scale). Every failure has a stable code, ALIGNAIR_<THING>_<STATE>; --error-format json prints it as JSON and --debug adds the traceback ( Error codes).

title: Training
body: Training reads are simulated with library flanks and, for a built-in germline set, novel alleles, so a model calls alleles it never saw from the set it is given. alignair train --init-from MODEL fine-tunes from a model ( Fine-tune a model); --data-workers simulates the training reads in parallel. alignair export turns a training snapshot into a model to share, with its card, and Aligner.push_to_hub uploads it with its card (Share your model). Aligner is the one way to predict, and run_training(TrainingConfig(...)) the one way to train. The supported names are exported from the alignair package ( Python API).

title: alignair genotype

title: alignair models

title: alignair models list

title: alignair models get

title: alignair models path

title: alignair models update
body: Downloads the latest version of an installed model, or of every installed model.

title: alignair models verify
body: Checks each cached model file against the checksum its registry lists, and prints OK, MISMATCH or UNKNOWN (not in registry) per version. It exits with status 1 on a mismatch.

title: alignair models prune
body: Removes old cached versions, keeping the newest of each model (--keep of them).

title: alignair info
body: Prints a model's card without loading the model; given an id, it downloads the model first if it is not cached (read a model's card).

title: alignair reference
body: Lists the built-in germline sets, or writes a model's germline set as FASTA. Its subcommands follow.

title: alignair reference list
body: Lists the germline sets built into GenAIRR, by the name alignair train --dataconfig takes.

title: alignair reference export
body: Writes a model file's germline set as one FASTA of its V, D and J alleles; --gapped writes each V IMGT-gapped, as Change-O's CreateGermlines.py needs. It takes a model file, so resolve an id with alignair models path (export a model's germline set).

title: alignair doctor
body: Prints what AlignAIR finds in your environment: the versions of Python and its dependencies, the GPU, and the cache and settings folders. It never fails (check the install).

title: alignair compare
body: Compares two AIRR tables of the same reads, gene by gene: how often the two tools call the same allele and the same gene, and, where they differ, how often the second tool's call is in the first's candidate set. It measures agreement, not accuracy (run both, then compare).

title: alignair analyze
body: Summarizes an AIRR table: the reads, productivity, gene usage, junction lengths, orientation, V identity, how complete the fields are, and a structural check.

title: alignair validate-airr
body: Checks an AIRR table's structure: the required columns are there, and positions and CIGAR strings stay inside the read. It is a quick check, not the AIRR Community's validator, which the airr Python package provides.

title: alignair train
body: Trains a model for a germline set: a built-in one (--dataconfig) or your own FASTAs ( --v-fasta, --d-fasta, --j-fasta, --chain-type). --plan checks the set and prints the plan without training; --init-from starts from an existing model. At the end it writes a model to share in bundle/ under --out. See Do I need to train?, Train a model and Fine-tune a model.

title: alignair export
body: Turns a training checkpoint into a model to share: a folder holding model.alignair, model_card.md, reference_manifest.json and, unless --no-validate, validation_report.json. alignair train already does this once at the end; use export for another checkpoint, or to record an id and version in the card ( Share it on Hugging Face).

title: alignair benchmark
body: Scores a model on reads GenAIRR simulates with known truth, per kind of read: a quick check of a model, with no other tool involved (Evaluate your model).

title: alignair demo
body: Trains a tiny model for a few steps, offline, and aligns simulated reads with it, with and without a donor genotype: it shows every step on your machine. Its calls are not accurate.

title: Records and the table
body: result.records holds one dict per read: AlignAIR's own record, not a row of the table. In it the read is turned forward, positions count from 0 with the end excluded, true and false are Python True and False, and the candidate set is v_calls, with its scores in v_likelihoods. write_airr turns the records into the AIRR table: positions from 1, T and F, rev_comp, v_call_set. title: Conventions
body: True and false are the AIRR strings T and F. A blank cell means unknown, not false; length_cropped is T or blank. In pandas, compare with "T" (filters). Fractions run from 0 to 1: the *_identity columns and mutation_rate. Positions in the read count from 1, both ends included, as AIRR defines them. When rev_comp is T, they count on the reverse complement of sequence. Lists are comma-separated: the alleles after the call in v_call, and the candidate sets. AIRR standard or AlignAIR's own. Every column follows the AIRR rearrangement schema except twelve that AlignAIR adds: productive_prediction, v_call_set, d_call_set, j_call_set, mutation_rate, orientation, input_sequence, segmentation_low_quality, length_cropped, airr_assembly_status, airr_assembly_reason and airr_assembly_error. Tools that read AIRR tables pass over columns they do not know. A --metadata join adds its own columns to these ( Join sample and cell metadata).

title: Model cards
body: The seven pretrained human models: the germline set each one calls from, how its alleles are named, how it was trained, and how to read a model's card yourself.

title: What every model holds
body: One locus of one species: human, and the locus in its id. Its germline set: every V, D and J allele with its sequence, the IMGT-gapped form of each V, and the position of the conserved codons that frame the junction (the V's Cys, the J's Trp or Phe). Every call is an allele of this set, unless you give another with --reference ( Use your own germline reference). What it learned from reads simulated with GenAIRR from that germline set: full-length reads and fragments, in all four orientations, with somatic hypermutation on the IG loci and none on the TCR loci. It reads at most 575 nt of a read. Its card: its id and version, the germline set, the allele counts and the training. The models are released under GPL-3.0-or-later, as the code is.

title: Germline sets and allele names
body: V alleles by their OGRDB labels: in IGHVF6-G21*07, F6 is the family and G21 the gene group. D and J alleles keep IMGT-style names (IGHD3-10*01, IGHJ6*02). , ], [ "IGK, IGL", "OGRDB's human IGK and IGL sets", <> OGRDB labels of their own, for V and J: IGKV1-5TCS*03, IGKJ2-27FL*01, IGLV6-A5V2*05, IGLJ2/3-HDWH*01. , ], [ "TRA, TRB, TRD, TRG", "IMGT's human sets", <> IMGT names: TRBV20-1*01, TRBD2*01, TRBJ1-2*01. , ], ] /> A genotype or a join table written in the other naming does not match: OGRDB and IMGT allele names says how to work with IMGT-named data on the IG models.

title: Notes per model
body: IGH, TRB and TRD call V, D and J; the others call V and J. A D is called only when AlignAIR finds at least 8 of its germline bases in the read; the TRD D alleles are 8, 9 and 13 nt long ( D calls on short D segments). IGH: two pairs of its D alleles have identical sequences (IGHD4-4*01 and IGHD4-11*01, IGHD5-5*01 and IGHD5-18*01); d_call names one of each pair. IGK and IGL are two models: a light-chain library is split by locus and each part aligned with its own model (Pick by locus). The TCR models were trained without hypermutation, as T cells do not hypermutate.

title: Error codes
body: Every error AlignAIR reports carries a code: what each code means and what to do, how to read an error, and how a pipeline or a script can catch one.

title: Read an error
body: The first line is the code, in brackets, and the message. Find the code in the table below: it says what to do. Context says where it happened: the command, the file, the model, the stage. Hint, when there is one, is the first thing to try. Here: download the model while online ( alignair models get alignair4-igh-human), then run offline. Errors go to standard error, never into the table. --debug adds the full traceback, which a bug report needs (Support).

title: The codes
body: Every code starts with ALIGNAIR_, then names what failed and how: ALIGNAIR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND, ALIGNAIR_GENOTYPE_ALLELE_NOT_FOUND. ALIGNAIR_ERROR is the general one. The code is the part meant for scripts: match on it, never on the message, whose wording can change. In Python, each code belongs to an exception class, shown under the code in the table; two classes can share a code (ConfigurationError and TrainingConfigError are both ALIGNAIR_CONFIG_INVALID). An error marked retryable may pass on a second try, such as a network failure ( ALIGNAIR_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE). The JSON form says it for each error.

title: JSON errors, for pipelines
body: --error-format json prints the error as one line of JSON on standard error, before or after the command's name: code, "The error code."], [message, "The message, for people."], [hint, <>What to try, or null.], [context, "Where it happened, as key and value pairs."], [category, <>The kind of failure: input, model, registry, ...], [exit_code, "The exit status the command returns."], [retryable, <>true when a second try may pass.], [type, "The Python exception class."], [schema_version, <>The version of this JSON form, 1.], ] /> With --debug as well, the traceback is one more field, traceback, of the same object.

The usage message says which; there is no code.", ], [ 70, <> An unexpected failure (ALIGNAIR_INTERNAL_ERROR): run it again with --debug and report it with the traceback. , ], [ 130, <> Interrupted, with Ctrl-C (ALIGNAIR_INTERRUPTED). , ], ] /> A status other than 0 does not always mean nothing was written: check the files the command names in its message.

title: Where models are kept
text: Cache, offline use and environment variables
body: A model you name by its id is downloaded once, from Hugging Face, into the cache, and read from there afterwards: ~/.cache/alignair (under $XDG_CACHE_HOME when it is set) , ], ["macOS", ~/Library/Caches/alignair], [ "Any", <> the folder in ALIGNAIR_CACHE_DIR, when it is set , ], ] /> alignair doctor prints yours as cache_dir. Inside, each version is one file, models/<id>/<version>.alignair, with its checksum beside it in a .sha256 file; alignair models path <id> prints a model's file. A download is written to a temporary file, checked against the SHA-256 its registry lists and only then moved into place, under a lock: a broken download never leaves a usable file, and jobs that share a cache do not overwrite each other's. A model loaded from its own Hugging Face repo (hf://org/repo) is kept in Hugging Face's cache instead (~/.cache/huggingface by default; Hugging Face's own HF_HOME moves it).

title: Work without a network
text: Cache, offline use and environment variables
body: Download the model on a machine with internet access, then run with --offline, which never touches the network: an id resolves to the newest cached version (or the version you pin), and a hf:// model to Hugging Face's cache. On a cluster whose compute nodes have no internet access, point ALIGNAIR_CACHE_DIR at a shared folder, run alignair models get once on a node that has access, and run the jobs with --offline. A model that is not in the cache stops the run with ALIGNAIR_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE.

title: The update notice
text: Cache, offline use and environment variables
body: alignair predict checks, at most once a day, whether the registry has a newer version of a model you have, and prints a line to standard error, such as ℹ alignair4-igh-human <version> available — run: alignair models update alignair4-igh-human. The check never delays or fails a run. --quiet, --offline, a pinned id@version or ALIGNAIR_NO_NETWORK turn it off.

title: Registries
text: Cache, offline use and environment variables
body: A registry is the catalog AlignAIR looks a model id up in: a registry.json file listing ids, versions and checksums, beside the model files. The default is the AlignAIR models on Hugging Face ( hf://AlignAIR/AlignAIR-pretrained). A lab can keep its own, and name it in one of three ways: --registry, repeatable, on every command that finds a model (registry= in Python); ALIGNAIR_REGISTRY, several separated by commas; registries in the settings file. The first of these that is set wins, and it replaces the default: list the default as well to keep the pretrained models. A registry is hf://org/repo (a public Hugging Face repo), https://host/path/ (a web server) or file:///path (a folder; a plain path works too). Registries are read without a token, so keep a private one in a shared folder or on a server your machines can reach. Share it on Hugging Face covers publishing a model.

title: Output columns explained
body: What the columns you read first say, how far each one goes, and how to keep only the rows your analysis can use.

title: The calls: v_call, d_call, j_call
body: v_call names the called V allele first. The alleles after it, comma-separated, match as many of the read's V bases as the call does, so the read alone cannot choose among them; IgBLAST lists equally scoring alleles the same way, and TIgGER and Change-O read the list as it is. read02 cannot tell IGHVF10-G42*01 from IGHVF10-G42*03. d_call and j_call name one allele each, with no list after it. The other D or J alleles AlignAIR weighed are in the candidate set (next section). Allele names. The IG models write OGRDB labels (IGHVF10-G50*02), the TCR models IMGT names; see OGRDB and IMGT allele names, and Map the labels to IMGT names to translate them. A blank call. A blank v_call means the read holds no V that AlignAIR could place (its row is partial, reason no_v). A blank d_call means the read shows no D, or AlignAIR found fewer than 8 of its bases (D calls on short D segments). locus is the model's locus, on every row. c_call stays blank: AlignAIR does not call the constant region, unless a metadata table fills it.

title: The candidate set: v_call_set, d_call_set, j_call_set
body: For each segment, the candidate set holds the alleles the model scored at least half as likely as its best one, best first, three at most. It is made before the read is aligned to the germline, and the call comes after that alignment. So the two can differ: the call can fall outside the set: the alignment can replace the model's first choice by an allele that matches more of the read's bases, such as a novel allele you bound with --reference; v_call can list more alleles than the set, as its list of equal matches has no limit. On a short read both happen. The last 150 nt of read01 (from FR3 to the J) match 17 V alleles equally well, the full read's allele (IGHVF10-G50*02) among them, while the set holds three alleles without it: Read the set as what the model weighed, not as a proof: several members mean the model could not settle on one allele; it is not exhaustive: it stops at three, and a read may support more alleles than that; one member does not by itself make a confident call: no other allele came within half the best's score; its members need not share a gene or a family, so collapse it to a gene only when every member has that gene. In Python, predict(threshold=0.5, cap=3) sets this rule (Python API). A donor genotype narrows both the call and the set to the donor's alleles.

title: The junction and productivity
body: junction, junction_aa, junction_length , <> The junction, as AIRR defines it: from the first base of the V's conserved Cys codon to the last base of the J's Trp or Phe codon. AlignAIR finds the two codons in the read itself. The junction is blank when either codon is not wholly inside the read, or the row has no V call. cdr3 is the junction without the two codons. , ], [vj_in_frame, <>T when the junction's length is a multiple of 3.], [ stop_codon, <> T when a stop codon lies in the junction's reading frame anywhere from the start of the V to the end of the J in the read. , ], [ productive, <> T when in frame with no stop codon, F otherwise, and blank when the read has no junction: blank means unknown, not unproductive. productive_prediction holds the same value. , ], ] /> All three read the junction's frame: vj_in_frame from the junction's length, and stop_codon from the codons in that frame between the V's start and the J's end. An indel inside the V or the J that shifts the frame is not seen (other limits ).

title: Identity and mutation
body: v_identity, d_identity and j_identity are the fraction of the aligned segment's bases that match the called germline, from 0 to 1, as AIRR defines them. IgBLAST writes a percentage: a filter "v_identity >= 98" becomes "v_identity >= 0.98". d_identity is blank for a D too short to call. mutation_rate is AlignAIR's estimate of the share of the read's V, D and J bases that differ from the germline, from 0 to 1. The model estimates it from the read; it is not counted from the alignment, so it need not equal 1 − v_identity. T cells do not hypermutate: on the TCR models an identity well below 1 points to sequencing errors or to an allele the germline set lacks (novel alleles).

title: Assembly status: is the row complete?
body: After the calls, AlignAIR builds the rest of the row: the IMGT-gapped alignments, the regions, the identities. Three columns say how that went: airr_assembly_status, <> complete: every field was derived. partial: some fields are blank, or ( j_cropped) the J call and junction rest on part of a J the cut shortened. failed: an unexpected error stopped the row; it keeps its calls. , ], [ airr_assembly_reason, <> Why a row is partial, such as no_v (no V call) or collapsed_segment. Every reason is explained in Partial rows. , ], [airr_assembly_error, <>The error that stopped a failed row.], [ segmentation_low_quality, <> T when the read's V or J region came out empty. Such a row is never complete, and its call for the empty segment means nothing. , ], [ length_cropped, <> T when the read was longer than 575 nt and only its first 575 nt were aligned; blank otherwise, never F (reads longer than 575 nt ). Cell Ranger's contigs often pass 575 nt, as they carry the constant region after the J: many 10x rows are T, and the cut usually takes only constant region, which AlignAIR does not call. A row cut inside its J is partial (j_cropped). , ], ] /> The console line counts the partial and failed rows, for example aligned 19 reads (0 dropped) -> out.tsv; 0 failed / 10 partial AIRR assemblies tagged. Only the full preset, the default, writes these columns ( Choose output columns).

title: Orientation: rev_comp, orientation, input_sequence
body: AlignAIR turns every read forward itself, so you never orient reads first. The table says how each one came: orientation, sequence, rev_comp, "Positions count on"] rows=[ ["forward", forward, "the read", F, sequence], [ "reverse-complemented", reverse_complement, "the read as given", T, <> the reverse complement of sequence , ], [ "complemented, or reversed", <> complement, reverse , <> the read turned forward (the read as given is in input_sequence) , F, sequence, ], ] /> rev_comp follows the AIRR convention, as IgBLAST's does: when it is T, every position and alignment refers to the reverse complement of sequence.

title: Keep the rows your analysis can use
body: The true/false columns (productive, rev_comp, vj_in_frame, stop_codon, segmentation_low_quality) hold the AIRR strings T and F, and a blank cell means unknown. length_cropped is T or blank, and blank means the read was not cut. Compare them with the string "T". First, with 10x contigs, keep the rows whose chain (Cell Ranger's, joined with --metadata) equals locus: a model gives reads of another locus rows that can look real (reads of another locus). Then, which rows to keep depends on the analysis: Rows with airr_assembly_status complete. , ], [ "The productive repertoire", <> Complete rows with productive T. , ], [ "Gene usage, genotyping (TIgGER)", <> Rows with a v_call, partial ones included, except those with segmentation_low_quality T. Count D and J on these rows only. On TCR rows, also leave out a low v_identity (below 0.9 here). , ], ] /> A complete row never has segmentation_low_quality T, so the first two filters need no check on it. It matters when you keep partial rows: there it marks the rows whose V or J call means nothing. A J call stands on a row without a V call, but that row is often a read of another locus. On 300 simulated TRA contigs aligned with the TRB model, counting J on every row with a J call (except segmentation_low_quality T) kept 277 meaningless TRBJ calls; the filter above keeps 4. T cells do not hypermutate, so a TCR row far from its germline is suspect: every simulated TRA and TRB contig aligned with its own model had a v_identity of at least 0.98, while the reads of another locus that got a V call had a median of 0.75 to 0.79. The 0.9 is an example: set it from your own rows. Any non-empty string is true in Python, so .astype(bool) turns every "F" into True. The filter ~table["segmentation_low_quality"].fillna(False).astype(bool) keeps no row at all. Compare with "T", or read the file with pd.read_csv(..., true_values=["T"], false_values=["F"]).

title: Every other column
body: The rest of the table follows the AIRR standard, counting as Change-O's MakeDb does where the standard leaves a choice: the IMGT-gapped sequence_alignment and germline_alignment, with N in the germline for the untemplated bases between the segments; each segment's start and end in the read and in its germline, 1-based and inclusive (the V's germline positions count in the IMGT-gapped V); the CIGAR strings, each over the whole read; the N regions (np1, np2); a row without a D call holds every base between V and J in np1; the framework and CDR regions, with their positions in the read. The output column dictionary describes all 99 columns, with their units and the presets that hold them; Choose output columns shows how to write fewer.

title: How far to trust the calls
body: Where AlignAIR's calls hold and where they do not: each known limit, how to spot it in the table, what to do about it, and when to check with IgBLAST.

title: What each row tells you about itself
