Its calls stand unless the row is partial (j_cropped: the cut fell inside the J).", ], [ <> A blank productive or junction , "The read does not hold both conserved codons: productivity is unknown.", ], [ <> A low v_identity, a high mutation_rate , "Heavy hypermutation, sequencing errors, an allele the germline set lacks, or a read of another locus.", ], ] />

title: Short reads and fragments
text: How far to trust the calls
body: A read that covers only part of its V holds fewer bases that tell alleles apart, so v_call lists more alleles. The junction is not affected. read06, whole and cut to its last 150 and last 100 nt: On the 150-nt fragment, the five listed alleles share one gene, so the gene call is safe. On the 100-nt fragment the list crosses families: the first name, IGHVF3-G6*03, is no more likely than the 67 after it. Shorter still, and the read has no V at all for AlignAIR: No V call. A read gets no V call when it shares no 15-nt stretch with any V allele of the germline set and its V alignment covers fewer than 20 bases or matches under 70% of them. Its row is partial with reason no_v; its D and J calls stand. The last 100 nt of read01 end this way. A read that ends before its J. Its J region comes out empty: the row has segmentation_low_quality T, is partial with reason collapsed_segment, and still carries a j_call, which means nothing. The first 200 nt of read01 get IGHJ1*01; the whole read is IGHJ6*02. No junction unless both conserved codons, the V's Cys and the J's Trp or Phe, lie wholly inside the read. What to do. Report fragments at the gene level when the listed alleles share a gene, and keep the whole list for TIgGER. Leave out rows with segmentation_low_quality T when you count gene usage, and use complete rows for junction and clone work ( filters).

title: Heavy hypermutation
text: How far to trust the calls
body: AlignAIR calls the V allele of the germline set that matches the most of the read's V bases. Somatic mutations can make a read match a sibling allele, one or a few bases away from the true one, as well or better: the sibling is then listed after the call, or becomes the call. The more mutations and the closer the siblings, the more often this happens. IgBLAST faces the same limit; the comparison measures both tools on it, as the mutation load rises (the "V allele siblings" suite). How it shows. A low v_identity, a high mutation_rate, and longer lists in v_call. What to do. Call from the donor's own alleles: a sibling the donor does not carry can then not be called (--genotype, or --infer-genotype to infer the genotype from the same reads; see Align with a donor genotype). Make allele-level claims on heavily mutated reads only after a cross-check; gene-level analyses are much less affected.

title: Reads longer than 575 nt
text: How far to trust the calls
body: A model reads at most 575 nt. A longer read is aligned on its first 575 nt, as written in the file, and its length_cropped is T. The cut comes before AlignAIR turns the read around: a forward read with a long stretch before its V loses its J and junction; a reverse-complemented read loses the start of its V. read01 with 300 extra bases in front of it is cut near the end of its V, before the junction: it gets no junction and no meaningful J call, and the row is partial (collapsed_segment). With about 200 extra bases the cut falls inside its J: the J call and the junction rest on part of the J, and the row is partial (j_cropped), even where the junction survived. What to do. Trim reads to the V(D)J region before aligning ( Prepare your input), and keep the complete rows: a row whose J ends before the cut stays complete. Cell Ranger's contigs are forward and carry the constant region after the J, so many are cut, mostly in the constant region, which changes no call; the few cut inside the J come out j_cropped.

title: Alleles that differ only outside the read
text: How far to trust the calls
body: Most reads show only part of their V: a primer inside the V cuts its start, and recombination trims its end. Alleles that differ only in the part a read lacks match it equally well, and v_call lists them all after the call; the first name is not more likely than the others. Alleles of different genes, even of different families, can be identical over a short stretch, as read06's last 100 nt show above. Alleles that differ only past IMGT position 318, at the very end of the V, can rarely be told apart in any rearranged read. D and J calls name one allele, with no such list. Two pairs of IGH D alleles have identical sequences ( IGHD4-4*01 and IGHD4-11*01, IGHD5-5*01 and IGHD5-18*01): d_call names one of each pair, so count each pair as one. d_call_set and j_call_set show the other alleles the model weighed. What to do. Collapse a list to a gene only when every allele in it has that gene. A donor genotype settles most lists: --infer-genotype re-calls the reads whose call falls outside the donor's genotype while their list holds an allele of it (infer the genotype).

title: D calls on short D segments
text: How far to trust the calls
body: The D is the least certain call. D alleles are short (11 to 37 nt in the IGH set; 12 and 16 nt in TRB; 8, 9 and 13 nt in TRD), recombination trims both their ends, and the N nucleotides around them can look like D bases. AlignAIR calls a D only when it finds at least 8 of the D's germline bases in the read. With fewer, d_call is blank, the D's place in the read (d_sequence_start, d_sequence_end) is kept and d_identity is blank. Either way, a row without a D call has no D in its germline: np1 runs from the V to the J, as Change-O reads such a row. With no D bases at all, the row has no D coordinates either. So a TRD D is called only when almost all of it remains: TRDD1*01 is 8 nt long. d_call names one allele; d_call_set lists the others the model weighed. What to do. Report D usage at the gene level, count the identical pairs above as one, and read a blank d_call as "too little D to call", not "no D". For a study that rests on D alleles, cross-check with IgBLAST. The comparison measures D calls as the D is trimmed shorter ("D observability").

title: Novel alleles
text: How far to trust the calls
body: AlignAIR calls only alleles of the germline set it runs with. A read of an allele the set lacks is called to the allele that matches it at the most bases, and its differences count as mutations: they lower v_identity and raise mutation_rate. Nothing in the row marks the allele as novel. AlignAIR does not discover novel alleles, and neither does --infer-genotype. Find them with a tool built for it, such as TIgGER, on AlignAIR's table ( TIgGER on AlignAIR's table). Then add them to the germline set with --reference: a read that matches the novel allele at more bases than the old call is called by the novel allele's name ( Novel alleles). Export the model's set with --gapped, append the novel alleles IMGT-gapped (TIgGER writes them so), and give that one file to AlignAIR, TIgGER and CreateGermlines. Read the warning that names any allele left without its anchor ( gaps and anchors).

title: Reads of another locus, and other sequences
text: How far to trust the calls
body: A model calls only its own locus, and every row carries that locus in locus. A read of another locus, or a sequence that is not a receptor at all, most often gets no V call: the row is partial with reason no_v, and still has a j_call, which means nothing. Most such rows have segmentation_low_quality F, so that column does not find them. And a fifth to a third of these reads come out as ordinary complete rows, with a V call of the model's locus, often a junction, sometimes productive T, and the run gives no warning. Simulated 10x-like contigs aligned with the model of another locus: no_v rows (with segmentation_low_quality T), <>complete rows, <>of them productive T] rows=[ ["300 TRA contigs, TRB model", "206 (23)", "85 (28%)", "21"], ["300 TRB contigs, IGH model", "246 (92)", "54 (18%)", "2"], ["300 TRB contigs, TRA model", "188 (4)", "98 (33%)", "13"], ] /> How it shows. Two signals tell these rows apart. With 10x data, Cell Ranger's chain (joined with --metadata) differs from locus. On the TCR models, v_identity is low: the off-locus rows with a V call had a median of 0.75 to 0.79, every true TRA and TRB contig 0.98 or more. A few off-locus reads keep only a short stretch of V that matches many alleles exactly, and reach a v_identity of 1: the chain column still finds those. What to do. Split mixed libraries by locus and align each part with its own model ( Pick by locus). Keep the rows whose chain equals locus, leave out TCR rows with a low v_identity, and count J only on rows with a V call (filters). Many no_v rows in a run point to reads of another locus, or to a genotype that misses genes.

title: Other limits
text: How far to trust the calls
body: Frameshifts inside V or J. productive is read from the junction: its frame and the stop codons in its frame. An indel inside the V or the J that shifts the frame is not, by itself, called unproductive. A genotype that misses alleles forces the reads of the missing alleles onto the nearest allele it allows, with nothing in the row to say so ( reads of genes the genotype leaves out). A germline set of another species binds to a human model when it has the model's segments, but how well the model calls it has not been measured ( references that are refused). Train a model for that species. Models from alignair demo or --preset quick are for trying the steps, not for results.

title: Partial rows and segmentation_low_quality
text: How far to trust the calls
body: A partial row keeps its calls but has some fields blank, or calls that rest on part of the read. airr_assembly_reason says why: no_v, <> The read holds no V AlignAIR could place (short reads ): a read that starts inside the junction, a D-J rearrangement, a read of another locus, or a read of a gene the --genotype leaves out. , "The D and J calls. No junction, alignment or regions.", ], [ nonproductive_indel, "The junction is out of frame or holds a stop codon, and AlignAIR estimates more than one insertion or deletion in the read: it does not build the read's alignment.", "The calls and the junction.", ], [ missing_calls_or_coordinates, "The V call, or the V or J position in the read, is missing.", "What was called.", ], [ collapsed_segment, <> The read's V or J region came out empty (segmentation_low_quality T): a read that ends before its J, or a long read cut short. , "The calls; the one for the empty segment means nothing.", ], [ incomplete_alignment, "The IMGT-gapped alignment could not be built.", "The calls, positions and junction.", ], [ j_cropped, <> The read was longer than 575 nt and the cut fell inside (or just before) its J ( long reads): the J call, the junction and FWR4 rest on part of the J. , "Everything a complete row has; the J call and the junction may be wrong.", ], ] /> A failed row met an unexpected error while its fields were built: airr_assembly_error holds the error, and the row keeps its calls and positions. Report one that repeats, with the read and --debug (Support). segmentation_low_quality is T on every row whose V or J region came out empty. Such a row is never complete: its reason is collapsed_segment, or one found before it, such as no_v.

title: The quality gates
text: How far to trust the calls
body: A run stops with an error when too many of its rows could not be assembled. The table is written either way, every row tagged; only the exit status (1) and the message report the breach. --max-assembly-failures, 0.01, "more than this share of the rows failed"], [--max-partial-assemblies, <>1.0 (never), "more than this share of the rows is partial"], [--permissive, "off", "never: the run always succeeds, rows still tagged"], ] /> A pipeline that should stop when the reads look wrong, say a library of another locus, can fail on partial rows too; a run on dirty reads can turn the gates off:

title: When to cross-check with IgBLAST
text: How far to trust the calls
body: Check a sample of the reads against IgBLAST when: a claim rests on V alleles of heavily mutated reads (lineages, mutation studies); a claim rests on D alleles; the reads differ from what the models were trained on: very long reads, unusual library designs, or a germline set of another species bound with --reference; the comparison shows IgBLAST ahead on a measure your analysis rests on. Give IgBLAST the germline set the model calls from, so both tools choose among the same alleles ( A fair side-by-side), then see where they agree: Agreement is not accuracy: on real reads neither tool is the truth. Look at the reads where they differ, and at whether IgBLAST's call is in AlignAIR's candidate set (the report's set rescue), which means shared doubt rather than a conflict.

title: Comparison with IgBLAST
body: How AlignAIR's calls compare with IgBLAST's on all seven loci, every measure shown, ties included; how that was measured, on simulated reads and on real IGH repertoires; and when IgBLAST is still the better choice.

title: The same germline set
body: IgBLAST's V, D and J databases are built from the model's own germline set, with an auxiliary file of J reading frames written from the same germlines, and IgBLAST runs with -organism human, -ig_seqtype Ig or TCR, and AIRR output (-outfmt 19). Both tools so choose among the same alleles. For a locus without D, IgBLAST gets a one-sequence placeholder D database, which it needs and does not search. The IgBLAST release is recorded, with checksums, alongside the results.

title: Simulated reads with known truth
body: GenAIRR simulates each read from known alleles, trims, N nucleotides, mutations and sequencing artefacts, so the truth of every read is known. Each read is scored on what it shows: a segment counts only when the read holds some of its germline bases; the right answer for an allele is the set of alleles a perfect aligner could defend from that read: the true allele and those that match the read as well over the bases it shows; a segment edge is right anywhere in its range of equally defensible positions; a missing call counts as wrong, except on a segment too short to call (fewer than 20 V, 8 D or 10 J germline bases), where abstaining counts as right. The reads come from a locked test split: generated from seeds never used while the models were developed, and scored once. Results from development runs are not shown. The models were trained on GenAIRR simulations too, so two parts of the comparison step outside them: a suite whose mutation model, N lengths and trims leave the defaults (S10), and the real repertoires below.

title: The 13 suites
body: [id, title, what]) /> IG reads carry somatic hypermutation; TCR reads do not, as T cells do not hypermutate. A suite or part of a suite that needs a D or hypermutation is left out on a locus without it: D observability runs on IGH, TRB and TRD, clonal lineages on the IG loci.

title: The measures
body: A measure's name is the segment, then what is scored. The tables show every measure the run compared; the main ones: v.top1_in_set, d.top1_in_set, j.top1_in_set , <>The called allele (the first one listed) is one the read supports., ], [v.gene_top1, "The called gene is right."], [ <> v.seq_start_exact, v.seq_end_exact, j.seq_start_exact, ... , "A segment's start or end in the read is exact. germ_start and germ_end do the same in the germline.", ], [ <> junction.nt_exact, junction.aa_exact, junction.length_exact , "The junction is exactly right, in nucleotides, in amino acids, in length.", ], [ clone_key.exact, "The V gene, the J gene and the junction length are all right: what clonal clustering groups on.", ], [ <> productive.correct, vj_in_frame.correct, stop_codon.correct , "The productivity calls are right.", ], [orientation.correct, "The read's orientation is right."], [ <> v.no_call, d.spurious_call, v_short.abstain_ok , "A missing call; a call for a segment the read does not hold; abstaining on a segment too short to call.", ], [ <> Names ending in _err, such as v.mutation_count_err , "A mean distance from the truth, in nucleotides or mutations: lower is better.", ], ] /> For the measures where lower is better (the _err measures, no_call, spurious_call, indel_false, germline_errors, outside_genotype and deleted_gene_call), a negative difference favours AlignAIR; the verdict already takes the direction into account.

title: Paired tests
body: Both tools are scored on the same reads. The difference is AlignAIR's score minus IgBLAST's, over the reads both were scored on, with its 95% confidence interval. The IgBLAST and AlignAIR columns are each tool's mean over the reads the measure applies to. A right-or-wrong measure is tested with an exact McNemar test, on the reads where only one tool is right; a measure in nucleotides or counts, with a paired z-test. The reads of one clone (S9) and the two strands of one read (S11) are not independent, so they are tested by cluster. The p-values of all the measures of one suite are corrected together (Holm, at 5%). The verdict is "AlignAIR better" or "IgBLAST better" when a difference survives the correction, and "tie" otherwise, which includes a measure with fewer than 10 paired reads.

title: Real IGH repertoires
body: Simulation is not the whole story, so the comparison also scores both tools on real human IGH repertoires where each donor's own alleles are known: The data. title: What AlignAIR does
body: Each B- or T-cell receptor chain is assembled from one V, one D (in IGH, TRB and TRD) and one J germline segment. The joins are trimmed and filled with non-templated (N) nucleotides, and B cells add somatic hypermutations on top. For each sequenced read, AlignAIR reports which V, D and J alleles it came from, where each segment sits in the read, the junction, and whether the rearrangement is productive: one row of an AIRR rearrangement table. Pick segments to see how the choice of V, D and J changes the read and its junction: The widget joins the segments without trimming or N nucleotides and uses IMGT-style names: it shows the idea, not a real read. The IGH model calls V alleles by their OGRDB names (below).

title: How AlignAIR works (optional)
body: For the curious: what happens between a read and its row in the table, in the model's own terms. You do not need this page to use AlignAIR.

title: The idea
body: AlignAIR learns alignment from reads simulated with GenAIRR, where the truth of every read is known: its alleles, the region of every base, its mutations, its conserved codons and its orientation. One model learns all of these tasks together. The paper in Nucleic Acids Research introduced this approach (multi-task deep learning for adaptive immune receptor alignment); this page describes the parts of the current models, as the code in src/alignair/network builds them. The model is a neural network: layers of simple functions whose numbers, the weights, were fitted during training. A read goes through it once, in one forward pass; exact alignment steps against the germline sequences then check and refine what it found, and plain rules build the AIRR row.

title: From a read to a row
Orientation
body: A read may come in any of four forms: forward, reverse complement, complement or reversed. Two signals decide. The k-mer vote counts, for each form, how many of the read's 12-base words occur in the bound germline set; when one form wins outright, it decides. Otherwise the orientation head decides: a head is a small output layer that answers one question from the model's features, here which of the four forms the read is in. The read is turned forward before anything else reads it.

title: Embedding and trunk
body: Each base becomes an embedding: a list of learned numbers that stands for the base and its position. The trunk then gives every base its features, once, for all the parts below to share. It is a stack of dilated convolutions: filters that look at a base together with bases 1, 2, 4, ... 32 positions away, twice over, so each base's features describe several hundred bases around it.

title: Parser and anchors
body: The parser cuts the read into its ordered regions: before V, V, N1, D, N2, J, after. It is a linear-chain CRF, a model that scores every allowed path through those regions and picks among them exactly; a path can skip a region (a light chain has no D, a fragment no start), but it can never put V after J. Two anchor heads find the conserved codons that frame the junction: the V's Cys and the J's Trp/Phe.

title: Mutation reader
body: The mutation reader says, for each base, how likely it is a germline base, a substitution or an insertion, and which column of the germline it lines up with. It never guesses the germline base itself, which would be memorizing the germline set: what the germline is comes only from the bound set.

title: The bank and its scans
body: The bank is the bound germline set laid out as rows, one per allele, of bases on fixed columns (IMGT-gapped for V). It is an input, rebuilt from whatever germline set the run uses, and not part of the weights. A scan scores every row of one segment's bank against the read: over the read's bases in that segment's region, a row gains where it has the read's base at the base's column, pays the cost of a mutation where it has another base, and pays a penalty where it has none. The scores become a probability for each allele. A donor genotype hides rows; a novel allele is a new row.

title: D presence
body: For loci with a D, a small classifier decides from the parser's and the D scan's evidence whether the read shows its D: absent, too short to call, or callable.

title: Refinement against the germline
body: Then come exact steps, with no weights: One locus per read, when a germline set holds several loci: the locus of the read's most likely V and J pair. V end and J start: from the anchors, the read is aligned to the called alleles' germlines, and each boundary moves to where the read stops following its germline. The D: the junction is aligned to every D allele, forward and inverted, and that alignment is combined with the D scan; the D's edges are then set on the called D's germline. The top five V alleles are re-scored by a banded gapped alignment, which follows an insertion or deletion the scan's columns cannot.

title: Calls and the AIRR row
body: Each allele's score is taken relative to the best. The candidate set (v_call_set and the others) keeps the alleles at least half as likely as the best, three at most. The read is then aligned to the called germline: an allele of the germline set that matches more of the read's V bases than the call replaces it, which is how a bound novel allele gets called, and the alleles that match exactly as many are listed after the call in v_call. Plain rules then build the row: the junction between the anchors, productivity, the IMGT-gapped alignments, CIGARs, identities and the FWR and CDR regions.

title: How the model learns
body: Training draws fresh reads from GenAIRR at every step; there is no fixed data set. Each read comes with its truth, and every part above has its own loss, a number that measures how wrong that part was on the read. Each loss is scaled to start near 1, and they are summed with equal weights, so no task is quietly turned down. Half of the time, the parts after the parser and the mutation reader are given the true regions and columns instead of the predicted ones (teacher forcing), so they learn from correct inputs early on. The reads are not all alike. A curriculum is a scale of difficulty, from clean reads to fully corrupted ones: more somatic hypermutation, sequencing errors and indels. Each training batch mixes reads from three points on that scale, reads with heavy hypermutation, and fragments that lost their 5' or 3' end; reads come in all four orientations, part of them with library flanks, and most of them productive. The TCR models' reads carry no hypermutation, as T cells do not hypermutate. Synthetic novel alleles, drawn by default, teach the scans to read an allele from the bound germline set rather than from memory.

title: Why the germline set is an input
body: The weights learned how to read a locus: where its regions are, what a mutation looks like, how a base lines up with a germline column. The alleles themselves sit in the bank, which each run builds from its germline set. So a donor genotype only hides rows, and a germline FASTA with novel alleles adds rows, both without training. A new locus or species is different: its regions and germlines look different from anything the weights learned, so it needs a model trained for it.

title: Read more
body: The paper: Konstantinovsky et al., Enhancing sequence alignment of adaptive immune receptors through multi-task deep learning, Nucleic Acids Research 2025, doi:10.1093/nar/gkaf651. How well this works, measure by measure: the comparison with IgBLAST, and where it does not: How far to trust the calls. Training your own: Train a model for your reference.

title: Do I need to train?
body: Decide whether to give a pretrained model your germline set or to train a model of your own, and what training costs.

title: Bind your germline set, or train
body: Use the pretrained model (Choose a model). , "No", ], [ "The same locus and species, but your germline set differs: novel alleles, a curated set, another release, IMGT's set for an IG locus", <> Bind it: --reference germline.fasta ( Use your own germline reference). , "No", ], [ "Calls only from one donor's alleles", <> --genotype (Align with a donor genotype). , "No", ], [ "Another species, a locus no model covers, or a germline set far from the model's", <> Train a model for it (Train a model for your germline set), or fine-tune a pretrained one (Fine-tune a model). , "Yes", ], ] /> "Far from the model's" has a concrete meaning. When you bind a FASTA, each V allele needs its IMGT gaps and the position of its Cys codon, and each J allele its Trp/Phe codon. AlignAIR takes the ones your FASTA does not give from the model's own alleles: the same sequence, or a V of the same length that differs at no more than 10% of its bases (how they are filled). A V allele unlike any of the model's gets its anchor only from its own IMGT gaps; without them it has none, and its reads get no junction. And a set of another species binds when it has the model's segments, but a human model calls another species' reads worse than a model trained or fine-tuned for it ( Mouse and other species). For another species, train or fine-tune.

title: Decide in four questions
body: Are your reads human, of a locus with a pretrained model? If not, train: no pretrained model has learned your species or locus. Is the model's germline set the one you want? If yes, use the model as it is. Check with alignair info alignair4-igh-human (its germline set and allele counts) or export the set with alignair reference export. Do you only need fewer alleles, one donor's? Give the genotype with --genotype. Do you need other or more alleles of the same locus? Bind your FASTA with --reference. Read the anchor warning it prints before the run: alleles it names have no anchor, and many of them mean your set is far from the model's. Give those alleles IMGT-gapped, or train. Not sure whether binding is good enough? Bind your set, align a sample of your reads, and compare the calls with those of the tool you use today on the same reads (alignair compare, see Evaluate your model).

title: What training costs
body: Training needs no sequencing data. It simulates its reads, with their true alleles and boundaries, from your germline set as it goes (with GenAIRR, which is installed with AlignAIR). What it needs is time on a machine. One step trains on one batch of simulated reads; a preset sets the number of steps, the batch size and how often the model is checked on held-out reads: quick, "300", "16", "4,800", "100 steps", "Checks that the run works, start to end. Its calls are not usable.", ], [desktop, "50,000", "64", "3.2 million", "2,000 steps", "The default."], [ full, "300,000", "128", "38.4 million", "5,000 steps", "A long run: nearly the pretrained models' steps, with twice their reads per step.", ], ] /> The seven pretrained models trained for 320,000 to 340,000 steps of 64 reads, 20 to 22 million reads in all (each one's card gives its count: Model cards). --steps, --batch-size and --val-every override a preset's numbers. How long a step takes depends on the machine. Three runs on one desktop (Intel i7-10700F with 8 cores, NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti), shared with other jobs; the times include the setup and the export: desktop preset, MOUSE_IGH_IMGT from scratch, 500 steps, --data-workers 6 , "GPU", "8 and 10 min in two runs: 1 to 1.2 s a step, so the preset's 50,000 steps would take 14 to 16 hours at that pace", ], [ <> MOUSE_TCRB_IMGT, warm start from the human TRB model, 100 steps, --data-workers 4 , "CPU", <> 3.5 min, VAL score 0.99 (the example) , ], [<>The same 100 steps from scratch, "CPU", "2.5 min, VAL score 0.47"], ] /> So a CPU is enough for --plan, quick and a short warm start from a model of the same locus; a desktop or full run from scratch wants a GPU. A warm start still trains the preset's full steps unless you lower --steps. The reads are simulated on the CPU while the model trains, so free CPU cores matter on a GPU machine too: --data-workers N simulates them in N worker processes (at most 28 are used), with the same reads as one process. To estimate your own time, time a short run with your preset's batch size and scale it by the steps: The time includes the setup and the export at the end, so it overstates a step a little. While it runs, a progress line every 50 steps ([50/500] loss …) shows the pace. Disk use is small: a training snapshot is a few MB, and a run keeps at most five of them. Next: Train a model for your germline set.

title: Train a model for your germline set
body: Train a model from a built-in germline set or from your own V, D and J FASTAs, check the plan first, and find the model it writes.

title: From a built-in germline set
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: alignair reference list lists the built-in sets, with filters by species and by locus or chain type: The T-cell sets are named with TCR, not the locus: MOUSE_TCRA_IMGT, MOUSE_TCRB_IMGT, MOUSE_TCRD_IMGT and MOUSE_TCRG_IMGT. A name such as MOUSE_TRB_IMGT is refused ([ALIGNAIR_CONFIG_INVALID] unknown GenAIRR dataconfig 'MOUSE_TRB_IMGT'). --chain takes the locus all the same: The sets come from IMGT for every species, and also from OGRDB for the human IG loci ( HUMAN_IGH_OGRDB, the pretrained IGH model's set). A model calls alleles by the names of the set it trained on: IMGT names from an _IMGT set, OGRDB labels from an _OGRDB set. Pick the naming your genotypes and downstream tools use. Then train: The command line uses the desktop preset unless you give --preset ( what each preset costs). Several names after --dataconfig train one model of several loci, for example --dataconfig MOUSE_IGK_IMGT MOUSE_IGL_IMGT for both light chains. For mouse T cells, a short warm start from the human model of the same locus gets much further than a run from scratch of the same length ( Fine-tune a model).

title: Check the plan first
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: --plan builds the germline set, checks the settings and prints what the run would do, in a few seconds, without training: the loci, the alleles per segment, whether there is a D, the longest read the model will read (576 positions), the model's size, and the steps and batch size. It does not estimate time or memory. A FASTA set that cannot be built is refused here, with the reason, before any training. Training also refuses to start when --out already holds a bundle/, so a model you have shared is never overwritten; choose a new folder or pass --overwrite.

title: From your own germline FASTAs
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: Give one FASTA per segment and the chain type. The D file is required for a chain with a D gene ( BCR_HEAVY, TCR_BETA, TCR_DELTA) and refused for the others ( BCR_LIGHT_KAPPA, BCR_LIGHT_LAMBDA, TCR_ALPHA, TCR_GAMMA).

title: Where germline FASTAs come from
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: OGRDB publishes germline sets for human, rhesus macaque, mouse (by strain), rainbow trout and Peromyscus leucopus (ogrdb.airr-community.org/germline_sets, a page per species), each as AIRR JSON and gapped or ungapped FASTA. An IGH set holds its V, D and J alleles in one file: split it by segment (below). Mouse IGK and IGL sets hold the V alleles of one strain; their J alleles are in the sets named "IGKJ (all strains)" and "IGLJ (all strains)". IMGT: the IMGT/V-QUEST reference directory ( imgt.org/vquest/refseqh.html) has one FASTA per species, locus and segment (IGHV.fasta, IGHD.fasta, IGHJ.fasta) of its functional, ORF and in-frame pseudogene alleles, V alleles IMGT-gapped. The sets are drawn from IMGT/GENE-DB. Your own set, from a genotyping study or a curated list.

title: What the FASTAs need
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: Headers. The allele name is the first word after > (OGRDB's headers are the name alone, >IGHV0-24BS*00). An IMGT header, fields joined by |, works as it is: the field with a * is taken as the name (IGHV1-11*01 in >AC090843|IGHV1-11*01|Mus musculus_C57BL/6|F|V-REGION|…). Names. GENE*ALLELE: the gene is the part before the *. A name given twice is counted as rejected, and its second sequence is dropped. Bases. A, C, G, T and N only, upper or lower case, with . for the IMGT gaps of a V. One allele with another letter, such as the ambiguity code Y, gets the whole set refused (IMGT's mouse IGHV set has two): [ALIGNAIR_CONFIG_INVALID] 216 refdata validation issue(s) (2 fatal, 214 curatable), then one line per fatal issue ([fatal] V allele 394 byte at position 226 is 0x59 ('Y') …). The message numbers the allele rather than naming it; this prints the headers of such alleles, to fix or remove: Gaps. Give the V alleles IMGT-gapped when you can: the gapped form gives GenAIRR the most to work with when it places each V's anchor. For example, OGRDB's C57BL/6 IGH set: save its "FASTA Gapped" download from the Mus musculus page as igh_gapped.fasta, split it into one file per segment by the letter after IGH in each name, and check the plan: The two warnings are normal for a FASTA set. The first says that the files name no species. The second counts findings of GenAIRR's checks of the set, such as a V allele whose Cys codon it could not place; the run goes on.

title: Check the anchors before you train
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: A read gets a junction only when its V and J alleles have an anchor in the model's germline set: the first base of the V Cys codon and of the J Trp/Phe codon. Count them from Python before you spend the training time; here, IMGT's mouse IGH set from the V-QUEST directory, without its two alleles with a Y: report.missing names the alleles without an anchor. Reads called to one of them get no junction: remove the ones you do not need, or accept it. After training, bundle/reference_manifest.json gives the same counts per segment (n and anchored; D alleles have no anchor). OGRDB's C57BL/6 IGH set above has all its V and J alleles anchored.

title: IMGT or OGRDB names
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: The model calls alleles by the names in your FASTA files, and keeps them. A genotype or a --reference you give the model later must use the same naming (a genotype in another one is refused, ALIGNAIR_GENOTYPE_ALLELE_NOT_FOUND). So train on the naming your genotypes, Change-O and TIgGER tables and gene-usage plots use. Allele names explains the two schemes.

title: Run the training
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: Remove --plan to train. A run prints the plan, then its progress: Every 50 steps, loss measures how wrong the model still is on its training reads; it falls as the model learns. At each check (every 2,000 steps with desktop), VAL score scores the model on a fixed set of held-out simulated reads, higher is better, and the best-scoring snapshot is kept. At the end, the best snapshot is exported as the model to use. Evaluate your model explains the scores. The quick preset trains 300 steps to show that a run works from start to end. Its calls are not usable. Train with desktop or full for a model you will make calls with.

title: Novel alleles, drawn by default
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: With a built-in set of one species, part of the training reads come from novel alleles that AlignAIR makes up as it goes: in each block of 4,096 reads, 40% of the V genes that allow it carry a new variant with 1 to 6 substitutions (the novel alleles line above counts them). This teaches the model to call an allele from the germline set it is given rather than from memory, which is what lets a bound set with your novel alleles work without training. The model's own germline set stays the one you trained on. A run from your own FASTA files draws none, because they name no species, and says so: novel alleles unavailable: novel alleles train a model of one named species; the reference names none (a custom reference); the run trains on the reference's alleles alone. In Python, TrainingConfig(novel_alleles=None) turns them off and a NovelAlleles(...) changes them (Python API).

title: Train from Python
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: TrainingConfig.from_genairr takes built-in set names or GenAIRR germline sets (as built from FASTA files above), a preset, and any setting to override (steps, batch_size, val_every, lr, seed, device, data_workers, …); it checks every value when it is built. run_training(config, output_dir=...) trains and returns a TrainingRun: model_path (the last snapshot), best_model_path (the best, when the model was checked), steps (the steps done), and best_aligner(), the best (or last) snapshot loaded as an Aligner, ready to predict. Give a preset, or set steps and val_every yourself: without them, a TrainingConfig trains 100,000 steps and never checks the model (val_every=0), so the run keeps no best snapshot. With data_workers above 0, call run_training under an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, as it starts worker processes. run_training writes the training snapshots but no bundle; export one with alignair export ( Share your model).

title: Resume an interrupted run (Python)
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: alignair train has no option to resume. From Python, resume_path continues a run from its latest snapshot: the newest model.step<N>.alignair beside the file you name. steps is the total to reach (here the preset's 50,000), and must be beyond the snapshot's step. The germline set and the model's settings must be the snapshot's; for a run from your own FASTA files, build the germline set again from the same files. Otherwise the resume is refused, with a hint to use init_from (Fine-tune a model). The weights, the optimizer's state and the random state carry on, but the resumed run's reads are not the ones the uninterrupted run would have drawn. A new output_dir keeps the first part's best snapshot apart: the resumed run keeps the best of its own checks. Export the one you choose with alignair export. resume_path and init_from cannot be given together. A training snapshot holds Python pickle sections, which run code when they are loaded: resume only from your own runs or ones you trust.

title: Use the model
text: Train a model for your germline set
body: Give the bundle's model file wherever a model id goes. Every option of alignair predict works with it, --genotype and --reference included: Next: Evaluate your model, then Share your model.

title: Fine-tune a model
body: Start a training run from an existing model's weights instead of from scratch, from the command line or from Python.

title: Start from a model
body: --init-from takes a model file, a pretrained model's id or a Hugging Face repo ( hf://org/repo). In Python, init_from takes a model file; resolve_model turns an id into the cached file, downloading it the first time. --plan works as before and shows the run's steps and batch size. A model from a Hugging Face repo needs pip install "alignair[hub]", and a private one a token in HF_TOKEN.

title: What a warm start does
body: Every weight of the new model whose name and shape match one of the source model's is copied; the rest start fresh, as in a run from scratch. The germline set is the one you train on. The source's alleles are not carried over, and the new model calls only the alleles of your set. The run starts at step 0 and trains for the preset's full number of steps (50,000 with desktop) unless you lower --steps, with a fresh optimizer and learning rate. Nothing of the source's training state is used. A model's weights do not depend on the alleles of its germline set, which it is given as an input. So between two models AlignAIR builds with its default settings, every weight is copied, whatever the species or locus, except the parts for the D gene when the source has none and the new model does (from an IGK model to an IGH one, for example): those start fresh. The run says how much it copied before it trains: A tensor is one block of the model's weights; the lines that follow (left out here) name the parts copied and the parts that start fresh.

title: When to try it
body: A related locus or species. You train a model for a germline set and a model of a related one exists: a mouse IGH model started from the human IGH model, or a strain's set started from a model of the species' wider set. A finished run, with other settings. Resuming continues a run only with its own settings and germline set; a warm start lets you train on from your model with another germline set, more steps or another learning rate.

title: Example: mouse TRB from the human TRB model
body: The mouse TRB set is MOUSE_TCRB_IMGT. A short warm start from the human TRB model, on a CPU, then a check of the model on fresh simulated reads: The same 100 steps without --init-from train from scratch. Both runs, measured on one desktop (Intel i7-10700F, 8 cores, shared with other jobs; the time includes the setup, the two checks and the export), and scored by alignair benchmark on its 200 clean reads (shares from 0 to 1): These are simulated reads, from one short run each: a sign of what a warm start saves, not a validated model. A model warm-started this way also called more J alleles right than the human model with the mouse set bound with --reference (Mouse and other species ). AlignAIR does not prescribe how long to fine-tune or with which settings. Start short, check the model with alignair benchmark, and train longer while its scores still rise. To compare a warm start with a run from scratch for your set, train both with the same settings and score them on the same reads (the same --n and --seed).

title: Resume or warm start?
body: The two cannot be combined. Resuming is described on Train a model for your germline set.

title: Evaluate your model
body: Score a trained model on simulated reads with known truth, compare its calls with another tool's on your reads, and check its output.

title: The validation report
body: A bundle has a validation_report.json (also listed in its card) unless it was exported with --no-validate: scores on a fixed set of simulated reads of the germline set the model trained on, at most 192 reads per set. They score the model's own pick, before AlignAIR's germline step refines the call; alignair benchmark scores the final calls. The entries to read first: v_allele_top1, d_allele_top1, j_allele_top1 , "Share of reads whose top allele is among the read's true alleles (the simulation can list several).", "Higher (0-1)", ], [ <> v_seg_mae, d_seg_mae, j_seg_mae , "Mean error of the segment's start and end in the read, in nucleotides.", "Lower", ], [ <> anchor_v_exact, anchor_j_exact , "Share of reads whose V Cys or J Trp/Phe codon is found at exactly the right base. The junction is built from them.", "Higher (0-1)", ], [orientation_acc, "Share of reads turned to the right orientation.", "Higher (0-1)"], [mutation_mae, "Error of the estimated mutation rate.", "Lower"], ] /> The other entries score single steps inside the model and matter mostly to developers. Expect D below V and J: D segments are short and trimmed at both ends, so many reads hold too little of the D to tell its alleles apart. The validation reads are simulated like the training reads. Good scores say the model learned the simulation; your reads still need their own check.

title: Score the calls: alignair benchmark
body: alignair benchmark simulates fresh reads with known truth from a germline set, aligns them as alignair predict does, and scores the calls, read group by read group: clean, "Full length, little hypermutation (mutation rate about 0.02) and few sequencing errors."], [moderate, "More of everything: mutation rate about 0.09, more sequencing errors and indels, ends lost."], [high_shm, "Heavy hypermutation (mutation rate 0.25). On a TCR locus the reads carry none, as T cells do not hypermutate."], [short_janchor, "Short reads that keep the J end and lose 150 to 350 nt of the 5' end."], ] /> Each group gets a row of the text report; --json writes the same numbers under these names: v, d, j (v_call_acc, …) , "Share of reads whose call (its first allele) is one of the read's true alleles.", ], [<>junc_nt (junction_nt_exact), "Share of reads whose junction is exactly right, base for base."], [<>junc_lenMAE (junction_len_mae), "Mean error of the junction's length, in nucleotides."], [ <> v_start_mae … j_end_mae (v_sequence_start_mae, …) , "Mean error of the V and J start and end in the read, in nucleotides.", ], [productive_acc, "Share of reads whose productive call matches the truth."], ] /> The reads depend only on the germline set, --n and --seed, so two models run with the same three are scored on the same reads: the way to compare a fine-tuned model with one trained from scratch. By default the reads are simulated from the first germline set the model's card names. A model trained from your own FASTA files has no built-in set to simulate from: give --dataconfig a built-in set whose allele names your model uses, or rely on its validation report.

title: Compare with another tool: alignair compare
body: On your own reads there is no truth, but there is agreement. Align the same reads with your model and with the tool you trust today, as AIRR tables, and compare them read by read: Set-rescue is the share of disagreements where the second table's allele is in the first table's candidate set (its v_call_set, d_call_set, j_call_set): shared ambiguity, not a conflict. So give AlignAIR's table as --a. The report ends with examples of the reads that disagree. Agreement is not accuracy: where the tools differ, either may be right. --json gives the numbers as JSON, --out writes the report to a file. Rows are matched by sequence_id, so both tables must name the reads alike. Allele agreement needs the same allele names, so align with the same germline set in both tools. Against a table of another germline set, or of genes only, such as Cell Ranger's airr_rearrangement.tsv or a MiXCR export, read the gene agreement column (an example on 10x TRB contigs).

title: Check the output: alignair analyze
body: alignair analyze out.tsv summarises a table your model wrote, in three parts. What to look for in a new model's output on your reads: orientation, indel-flagged reads, mean V identity, and completeness: the share of rows with v_call, j_call, junction, cdr3 , <> A junction share well below the v_call share points to alleles without an anchor (see reference_manifest.json); a low V identity to reads far from your germline set. , ], ["VALIDATION", "required AIRR columns, coordinate and junction-length checks", <>Ends with => VALID.], ] /> --json gives the report as JSON. For how far the pretrained models' calls can be trusted, and how they were measured, see How far to trust the calls and the comparison with IgBLAST.

title: Share your model
body: Turn a training run into one model file others can run, put it on Hugging Face, and load it back by name.

title: Export the model: alignair export
body: alignair train already exported its best snapshot to bundle/. Run alignair export yourself when you trained from Python (run_training writes no bundle), to export another snapshot, or to record a name and version in the card: The folder gets the same four files as a run's bundle/: model.alignair, model_card.md, reference_manifest.json and validation_report.json. The export scores the model on the validation reads (--no-validate skips that; the card then says the scores are pending), checks that the new file loads, and refuses a folder that exists unless you pass --overwrite. A training snapshot (model.alignair, model.step<N>.alignair or model.best.alignair in the run folder) holds its training state as Python pickle sections, which run code when they are loaded. The exported model has none and loads without running any code. For a run from your own FASTA files, the export reads the germline set from the snapshot's pickle section, and says so: export only snapshots you trust.

title: Put it on Hugging Face
body: Aligner.push_to_hub uploads the model file, with the model_card.md and reference_manifest.json beside it, to a Hugging Face model repo in one commit. It needs pip install "alignair[hub]" and a Hugging Face token with write access, given as token= or in HF_TOKEN. It is Python only. Private by default. A repo it creates is private unless you pass private=False. A repo that exists keeps its visibility; change it on Hugging Face. It refuses a training snapshot (the message names alignair export), and an Aligner made by with_genotype or bound_to, which is not a file. filename= names the file in the repo (model.alignair by default), and revision= commits to a branch. aligner.save_pretrained("folder") copies the model file to a folder instead.

title: Load it back
body: hf://org/repo works wherever a model id does. It needs alignair[hub]; a private repo also needs a token (--hf-token, token=, or HF_TOKEN). --revision, or @revision after the name, pins a branch, tag or commit. alignair info hf://your-org/alignair-mouse-igh prints its card, and --init-from hf://your-org/alignair-mouse-igh fine-tunes from it. The download is kept in Hugging Face's own cache (~/.cache/huggingface by default), not AlignAIR's, and --offline reads it from there (Cache, offline and environment variables).

title: The model's licence
body: AlignAIR and its pretrained models are released under GPL-3.0-or-later, and the card AlignAIR writes for a model you train says so, with how to cite AlignAIR. A model also holds its germline set, which keeps the terms of its source (OGRDB, IMGT, or yours): read them before you share a model, and add them to model_card.md.

title: The pretrained catalog
body: The models named by id, such as alignair4-igh-human, live in AlignAIR's shared catalog, which the maintainers publish (Publishing to the catalog). To propose a model for it, open a "Model or reference request" issue (Support).

title: Choose a model
body: Pick the pretrained model for your locus, know which allele names it writes, and get it ready to run offline.

title: Pick by locus
body: A model calls one locus, so use the model of the locus your reads come from: heavy chains with alignair4-igh-human, beta chains with alignair4-trb-human, and so on. The light chains are two loci with a model each: kappa (alignair4-igk-human) and lambda ( alignair4-igl-human). A library that holds several loci, such as the heavy and light contigs of one 10x run, is aligned once per locus, each part with its own model. Split the reads by locus first when you can (a 10x filtered_contig_annotations.csv names each contig's locus in its chain column). A model calls only alleles of its own locus, so the calls it gives a read of another locus mean nothing, even when the row looks complete. For 10x TCR contigs, the whole recipe (split by chain, one model per chain, the annotations carried, the chains paired by cell) is on Join sample and cell metadata.

title: What a model contains
body: A model is one file. It holds: what it learned from simulated reads of its locus: full-length reads and fragments, in any orientation, with somatic hypermutation on the IG loci. It reads at most 575 nt of a read; its germline set: every V, D and J allele with its IMGT-gapped form and the position of its conserved anchor (the V Cys and J Trp/Phe codons). The IG models carry OGRDB's human sets (for IGH, OGRDB V8), the TCR models IMGT's. Every call is an allele of this set, unless you give another set with --reference; a card: its id, version, germline set, allele counts and how long it trained. It aligns single reads: merge paired R1/R2 reads before aligning. BAM and CRAM files are not read. The models are released under GPL-3.0-or-later, as the code is. Each model's full card is on Model cards.

title: Allele names: OGRDB and IMGT
body: The IG models call alleles by their OGRDB labels, the TCR models by their IMGT names: IGH: V alleles are labelled IGHVF…-G…. In IGHVF6-G21*07, F6 is the family and G21 the gene group. IGH D and J alleles keep IMGT-style names (IGHD3-10*01, IGHJ6*02). IGK and IGL: OGRDB labels of their own, for V and J alike, such as IGKV1-5TCS*03, IGKJ2-27FL*01, IGLV6-A5V2*05 and IGLJ2/3-HDWH*01. TRA, TRB, TRD, TRG: IMGT names (TRBV20-1*01). So a table from an IG model will not join on v_call with one IgBLAST wrote against IMGT's set, a gene-usage plot shows OGRDB labels, and a genotype written in IMGT names is refused ( ALIGNAIR_GENOTYPE_ALLELE_NOT_FOUND). You have two ways to work with IMGT-named data: call with IMGT's set, or map the model's labels to IMGT names.

title: Call with IMGT's set
body: Bind IMGT's germline set with --reference, and the calls carry IMGT's names. Immcantation's germline files (IMGT/GENE-DB, one FASTA per segment) are read as they are, headers included: The junctions of all 20 example reads are unchanged, and so are their D and J calls but one: read10's J becomes IGHJ6*04, an allele IMGT's set has and the model's lacks. A warning before the run names any allele whose anchor could not be placed.

title: What the IG sets lack
body: OGRDB's sets hold fewer alleles than IMGT's. The IGH model has 198 V, 33 D and 7 J alleles; IMGT's human IGH set (as GenAIRR ships it, pseudogenes and ORFs included) has 307, 47 and 14. The model lacks these J alleles: IGHJ3*01, IGHJ4*01, IGHJ4*03, IGHJ5*01, IGHJ5*04, IGHJ6*01 and IGHJ6*04. A read of an allele the set lacks is called to the nearest allele it holds, usually another allele of the same gene (IGHJ6*04 becomes IGHJ6*02), and its identity stays below 1 even when the read is unmutated. On 3,000 simulated unmutated reads drawn from IMGT's set: fewer than 2% of the reads of a J allele the model lacks got j_identity 1, against over 99% of the reads of a J it holds; with IMGT's set bound, 1,288 of the 1,305 reads of a V allele the model lacks got their V allele back, but only 589 of the 1,503 reads of a missing J allele got their J allele.

title: Map the labels to IMGT names
body: OGRDB's current human sets, at ogrdb.airr-community.org/germline_sets, name their alleles by their IUIS (IMGT) names (an allele IUIS has not named carries an i, as in IGHV3-30*i02), and they hold the IGH model's sequences: each of its 238 alleles has the same sequence, or one containing it, in OGRDB's IGH_VDJ set (release 10). So matching sequences gives each label its IMGT name. Export the model's set, download OGRDB's "FASTA Ungapped" of the same locus (here saved as ogrdb_igh.fasta), and match them with this script: names.tsv translates either way: an IMGT-named genotype or gene-usage table into the model's labels, or AlignAIR's calls into IMGT names. For IGK and IGL it is partial: about half of the model's alleles find a name this way (83 of 176 for IGK, 100 of 191 for IGL).

title: First use, the cache and offline use
body: The first run with a model id downloads the model from Hugging Face, checks its SHA-256 and keeps it in the cache: ~/.cache/alignair on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/alignair on macOS. Set ALIGNAIR_CACHE_DIR to put it elsewhere, a shared directory on a cluster for example. No login is needed. Later runs read the cached file. (A model from a Hugging Face repo, hf://org/repo, public or private, needs pip install "alignair[hub]"; the ids above do not.) To run where there is no internet (a compute node, a plane), download the model ahead on a machine that has it, then run with --offline, which never touches the network: alignair4-igh-human@<version> pins a version (alignair models list shows the latest). Every run records the model id, version and file checksum it used in out.tsv.run.json, beside the table. More on Cache, offline and environment variables.

title: List the models and read a model's card
body: alignair models list lists every model id with its latest version and whether it is installed, available, or has an update. alignair info prints a model's card without loading it; given an id, it downloads the model first if it is not cached: The card also shows when the model was made, how many steps it trained and a fingerprint of its allele order. alignair info alignair4-igh-human --json prints all of it as JSON.

title: Mouse and other species
body: The pretrained models are human. --reference binds another germline set of the same species and locus, or your novel alleles; it does not make a human model call another species well. For mouse or any other species, train a model on its germline set, or fine-tune the human model of the same locus on it ( Fine-tune a model). On 300 simulated mouse TRB reads: The built-in germline sets to train on are named by species, locus and source, with TCR for the T-cell loci: MOUSE_IGH_IMGT, MOUSE_IGK_IMGT, MOUSE_IGL_IMGT, MOUSE_TCRA_IMGT, MOUSE_TCRB_IMGT, MOUSE_TCRD_IMGT and MOUSE_TCRG_IMGT, with a C57BL/6J set beside each. alignair reference list lists them: To fine-tune the human TRB model on the mouse set, check the plan first: --plan prints what the run would do, without training. Drop it to train. The fine-tune in the table above ran 100 steps (--steps 100), not the preset's 50,000: about 200 s on the CPU of an 8-core desktop (Intel i7-10700F, --data-workers 4). Check a model you trained with Evaluate your model before you rely on it.

title: Prepare your input
body: What AlignAIR reads, what it does with read ids and unusable reads, and how to give it a table or a stream.

title: Formats
body: --input takes FASTA (.fasta, .fa, .fna), FASTQ ( .fastq, .fq), a CSV or TSV table with a sequence column, or plain text with one read per line; any of them gzipped (.gz). The format comes from the file name, else from the first line. FASTQ qualities are read but not used. AlignAIR aligns single reads, full-length or fragments, in any orientation: it finds the orientation itself and reports it in rev_comp and orientation. Merge paired R1/R2 reads before aligning (pRESTO's AssemblePairs, fastp or vsearch, for example). BAM and CRAM files are not read.

title: Read ids
body: A read's id is the first word of its FASTA or FASTQ header, or a table's id column. A read without one gets seq and its position in the file, counted from 0 (seq7). Every read is kept, even when its id repeats: the second read01 becomes read01_dup1, the third read01_dup2. For a FASTA whose reads are named read01, read02 and read01 again, the first column of the table is: A metadata join still matches both reads to the table's read01 row, because it uses the id as the input file gave it.

title: Reads that are dropped
body: Each read is upper-cased, and the IUPAC ambiguity codes (R, Y, S, W, K, M, B, D, H, V) are read as N. Any other character (a gap, a digit, punctuation) is unusable: it is read as N too, but a read in which more than 20% of the characters are unusable is dropped, and so is an empty read. The console line counts them, and --rejects-out writes them to a table with the reason: position counts from 0. If every read is dropped, the run stops with [ALIGNAIR_INPUT_INVALID] no valid reads in reads.fasta: check the file's format first.

title: Reads longer than 575 nt
body: A model reads at most 575 nt. A longer read is aligned on its first 575 nt, as the read is written in the file, and its row says length_cropped = T (the cell is blank for a read that was not cut). The cut happens before AlignAIR orients the read, so which end is lost depends on the read's orientation: a forward read loses its 3' end. That is often only constant region; but when much sequence comes before the V (a long leader, UTR or primer), the J and the junction can be lost; a reverse-complemented read loses the 5' end of the molecule: the start of the V. Its J and junction are kept, and its V alignment starts further into the germline. A cut that falls after the J changes nothing AlignAIR reports. A cut inside the J leaves only part of it, and the J call, the junction and FWR4 rest on that part, so AlignAIR marks the row partial with airr_assembly_reason = j_cropped (its J alignment runs to the last base read). A cut before the J leaves the row partial too (collapsed_segment, or j_cropped when a few bases still align as J). In a test that put 100 to 320 nt of random sequence before four example reads, all 40 rows whose junction changed came out partial (25 j_cropped, 15 collapsed_segment), as did 12 rows cut inside the J whose junction survived; none of the 40 rows whose J ended before the cut did. So the usual filter drops them: When there are many, trim the reads to the V(D)J region before aligning (remove the leader, primers and constant region in your preprocessing). 10x contigs. Cell Ranger's contigs carry the 5' UTR and leader before the V and part of the constant region after the J, so many run past 575 nt and come out length_cropped = T. That is expected: the contigs are forward, and the cut usually takes only constant region, which AlignAIR does not call (c_call comes from Cell Ranger's annotations, through --metadata). In a test with 300 simulated TRB contigs given 10x-like flanks (80 to 160 nt before the V, 100 to 250 nt after the J, of random sequence), 271 came out cropped; every one kept the V call, J call and junction of the same contig without flanks, and none was cut inside its J. Contigs with a longer stretch before the V are the ones that come out j_cropped.

title: Reads from pRESTO: CONSCOUNT and DUPCOUNT
body: A read's id is the first word of its header, so a pRESTO header such as >read01|CONSCOUNT=2|DUPCOUNT=5|PRCONS=IGHG becomes the whole sequence_id, and its annotations do not become columns, as they do with Change-O's MakeDb. To get MakeDb's consensus_count and duplicate_count, split the headers into a plain id and a table of the annotations, then join the table with --metadata: The first command writes reads.fasta with plain ids and annotations.tsv with one row per read. Another annotation goes the same way: add it to the awk and to --keep-columns. Without --keep-columns, the two counts are kept and prcons is not ( which columns are kept).

title: Read from standard input
body: --input - reads standard input, so AlignAIR can sit at the end of a pipe. The format comes from the first line (> for FASTA, @ for FASTQ). --infer-genotype reads its input twice, so it needs a file, not -. In Python, pass the reads as a list of strings to predict.

title: Read a table
body: In a CSV or TSV table, AlignAIR takes the sequence from a column named sequence, seq, nucleotide or read (any case), and the id from one named sequence_id, id or name. Name other columns with --sequence-column and --id-column. A .tsv file, or one whose header has a tab, is read as tab-separated; any other as comma-separated. Without --sequence-column, this table is refused: [ALIGNAIR_INPUT_INVALID] no sequence column in reads.csv; expected one of ('sequence', 'seq', 'nucleotide', 'read') or select the sequence column explicitly . The table's other columns are not carried into the output; to carry them, give the same table to --metadata as well (Join sample and cell metadata).

title: Align with a donor genotype
body: Call each read only from the alleles one donor carries, from a genotype you have or one AlignAIR infers from the reads.

title: The genotype file
body: A genotype is a YAML or JSON file keyed by segment, V, D and J (either case), each listing allele names of the model's germline set. A segment the file does not name keeps all its alleles. With the IG models, the names are OGRDB's labels (see Allele names). The same in JSON is `"V": ["IGHVF10-G50*02", ...], "J": ["IGHJ4*02", ...]`. To see the names a model knows, export its germline set (alignair reference export, on Use your own germline reference) and list the FASTA headers.

title: Reads of genes the genotype leaves out
body: With a YAML or JSON genotype, every call of a segment it names comes from its alleles, so the genotype must hold every allele the donor carries. Here is the genotype above, which names 4 V alleles, on the 20 example reads, without it and with it: IGHVF10-G50*02, IGHJ6*02, <>IGHVF10-G50*02, IGHJ6*02, "0.959, 0.959", "complete", ], [ "read02", <>IGHVF10-G42*01,IGHVF10-G42*03, IGHJ4*02, <>IGHVF10-G42*01, IGHJ4*02, "0.969, 0.969", "complete", ], [ "read04", <>IGHVF9-G32*01, IGHJ5*02, <>IGHVF10-G50*02, IGHJ4*02, "0.955, 0.790", "complete", ], [ "read07", <>IGHVF1-G2*01, IGHJ3*02, <>no V call, IGHJ6*02, "0.956, blank", <>partial, no_v, ], ] /> read01 carries an allele of the genotype: its call is unchanged. read02's tie is settled: IGHVF10-G42*03 is not in the genotype. read04 is a read of a gene the genotype leaves out. It is called to the closest allele the genotype allows, and its row is still complete. Its J is forced the same way. What gives the forced call away is its identity: v_identity falls from 0.955 to 0.790, and j_identity from 1.0 to 0.914 (spot a forced call). read07 matches no allowed V allele closely (under 70% identity over its V, and no 15-nt stretch in common with any of them). It gets no V call, its D and J calls stand, and its row is partial with airr_assembly_reason no_v. A read of an allele the genotype leaves out is called to the nearest allele it allows, or gets no V call. Use a genotype that covers every gene the donor expresses. Many no_v rows mean the genotype misses genes, or the reads are of another locus. Partial rows never fail the run by default; the console line counts them ( aligned 20 reads (0 dropped) -> out.tsv; 0 failed / 2 partial AIRR assemblies tagged).

title: Spot a forced call
body: A forced call matches the read less well than its true allele would, so its v_identity drops. Align the reads once without the genotype and once with it, and compare the two read by read: On the example reads this finds read04 (0.955 to 0.790), read10 (0.962 to 0.841), read11 (0.969 to 0.843) and nine more of the reads whose gene donor.yaml leaves out; two more forced calls drop by less than 0.05, so choose the threshold for your data. Within one run, rows whose v_identity sits far below the other rows of their gene point the same way.

title: When a genotype is refused
body: A genotype that names an allele the model's germline set does not hold is refused before any read is aligned: Here the genotype uses IMGT names on an IG model. Write it with the model's labels instead ( map the names), or bind a germline set that holds these names with --reference: IMGT's set, or the model's own set plus your novel alleles. The genotype can then name them. The other refusals: is keyed by gene names (IGHV3-23: [...]), <> ALIGNAIR_CONFIG_INVALID: donor.yaml is keyed by gene names (IGHV3-23); its keys are segments (V, D, J), each listing allele names , ], [ "is not YAML or JSON (a FASTA, say)", <> ALIGNAIR_CONFIG_INVALID: donor.fasta is not a YAML or JSON genotype: ... (a FASTA goes to --reference) , ], [ <>gives a segment an empty list (V: []), <> ALIGNAIR_INPUT_INVALID: the genotype leaves gene V with no allele , ], ] /> In Python, load_genotype and with_genotype raise the matching errors ( UnknownAlleleError for an allele the set lacks). Every code is on Error codes.

title: A genotype from an AIRR table: alignair genotype
body: alignair genotype infers a donor's V genotype from any tool's AIRR table, by a frequency rule like that of TIgGER's inferGenotype. For each V gene it counts the rows whose v_call is a single allele (a tie counts for none). The gene keeps its most frequent alleles until they explain 87.5% of those rows (--explain; TIgGER's default share too). It writes an AIRR GenotypeSet; --locus sets its locus (default IGH). Two things differ from TIgGER: it counts every single-allele row, mutated or not, where inferGenotype by default counts only unmutated reads. Somatic mutations can move a read onto a sibling allele, and those reads count here; a gene with fewer than 10 such rows (--min-reads, AlignAIR's own cutoff, not TIgGER's) is left open: no evidence, so no genotype for it. On a mutated B-cell repertoire, compare a few genes with TIgGER's genotype, or keep only the rows with a low mutation_rate in the table you give alignair genotype (it reads any AIRR table). (The 20 example reads are far too few; a repertoire of thousands of reads genotypes most genes.) A genotyped gene prints its alleles, such as IGHVF3-G9: IGHVF3-G9*03, IGHVF3-G9*01. --genotype reads the GenotypeSet as it is, so the round trip is one more run: A GenotypeSet restricts only the genes it names: a gene it left open keeps all its alleles (TIgGER's reassignAlleles, by contrast, moves the reads of genes its genotype leaves out). A YAML or JSON genotype is stricter: each segment it names is limited to the alleles it lists.

title: Infer the genotype in the same run: --infer-genotype
body: --infer-genotype does both steps in one run, in two passes over the file. Pass 1 aligns every read and infers the V genotype by the same rule. Pass 2 re-calls only the reads whose call the genotype excludes while their v_call lists an allele it allows; an open gene keeps all its alleles. D and J calls are not changed. The genotype is written to --genotype-out (default out.tsv.genotype.json), the same GenotypeSet alignair genotype writes. --genotype-explain (0.875) and --genotype-min-reads (10) set the rule. The input is read twice, so it must be a file, and all its reads should come from one donor. It cannot be combined with --genotype. It genotypes V only. It does not find novel alleles, mark deleted genes or separate donors. The Python API has no inferring pass; run it from the command line.

title: Use your own germline reference
body: Call from your own germline set, novel alleles included, with a pretrained model and no training.

title: What the FASTA needs
body: Every segment the model calls. V, D and J alleles for the IGH, TRB and TRD models; V and J for IGK, IGL, TRA and TRG. Names that show their segment. The first word of each header is the allele's name. The segment is read from the letter after the locus code (IGHV1-2*02 is V, TRBJ2-1*01 is J), else from the one V, D or J letter in the name. An IMGT/GENE-DB header, as in Immcantation's germline files (>X00369|IGHV3-11*04|Homo sapiens|F|V-REGION|...), is read as it is: the allele's name is its first | field that holds a *, as Change-O reads it. One sequence per name. A name given twice with two sequences is refused. Gapped or not. Sequences may be IMGT-gapped (with . or -) or ungapped. A gapped V keeps its gaps. Gapped is best: Change-O's CreateGermlines.py and TIgGER need the V alleles gapped, and a gapped V needs no gaps filled in (see below).

title: One germline file for the whole analysis
body: The easiest start is the model's own set, exported gapped, to which you add your novel alleles (TIgGER's novel alleles, the novel_imgt sequences of findNovelAlleles, are already gapped): Then give the same germline.fasta to every tool downstream: to TIgGER as its germline set, and to CreateGermlines.py (-r germline.fasta), which reads AlignAIR's table as it is. The gapped export alone calls exactly as the model's own set does, and an ungapped novel allele binds too, but CreateGermlines.py needs it gapped.

title: Novel alleles
body: A V allele of your set that matches the read at more bases than the model's call becomes the call, so a novel allele the read supports is called by its own name. For example, add to the IGH set a novel allele of IGHVF10-G50*02 with two substitutions, named the TIgGER way: read01 carries both substitutions and is now called to the novel allele; the other reads are unchanged. A genotype can name the novel allele once it is in the bound set.

title: How missing gaps and anchors are filled
body: Each V and J allele needs its anchor (the first base of the V Cys or the J Trp/Phe codon), and each V its IMGT-gapped form. AlignAIR fills what your FASTA does not give, in this order: what the FASTA gives: a gapped V keeps its gaps; the model's allele with the same sequence: its gaps and anchor; for a V, the model's allele of the same length that differs at the fewest bases, when that is at most 10% of them: its gaps and anchor (this is how the novel allele above got its own); else, a V's anchor from its own IMGT gaps, and a J's from its one F/W-G-X-G motif. Alleles left without an anchor are named in a warning before the run: Here a novel V with a 3-nt insertion was given ungapped, so no rule could place it. Give such an allele IMGT-gapped, and check its sequence.

Give all the segments (alignair reference export writes the model's own), or use the model of your set's locus. , ], [ <>holds alleles of another locus besides the model's (IGH and IGK together), <> Refused: [ALIGNAIR_CONFIG_INVALID] the reference holds alleles of IGK, a locus the model does not call (it calls IGH) . Rename them. , ], [ "is of another species", <> Not checked: it binds when it has the model's segments, but a human model calls another species' reads worse than a model trained or fine-tuned for it ( Mouse and other species). , ], ] />

title: Export a model's germline set
body: alignair reference export writes a model file's germline set as one FASTA of its V, D and J alleles (238 for the IGH model). It takes the model file, so resolve an id to its cached file first with alignair models path, which downloads the model if needed. --gapped writes each V IMGT-gapped, as Change-O's CreateGermlines.py needs; D and J are written as they are. With a --reference run, the germline set to give downstream tools is your FASTA, not this export (one germline file).

title: Join sample and cell metadata
body: Carry cell barcodes, UMI counts, sample ids or any other per-read column from a side table into the AIRR table.

title: A 10x example
body: --metadata joins a CSV or TSV table to the reads by read id. With Cell Ranger's output, the contigs go to --input and the annotations to --metadata. Cell Ranger's contig file holds every chain of the run, and a model calls one locus, so give each model the contigs of its own chain ( contigs_IGH.fasta here; the next section shows the split): The annotation columns follow AlignAIR's own (first row shown, a few columns): Cell Ranger's barcode, umis, reads and c_gene are also written under their AIRR names, cell_id, umi_count, consensus_count and c_call, which Change-O, SCOPer and Scirpy read. The metadata is carried as given; it is not checked against the calls.

title: 10x TCR contigs, chain by chain
body: A model of one locus gives reads of another locus rows that look real. Of 300 simulated TRA contigs aligned with the TRB model, 85 came out complete with a TRBV call and 21 productive, and the run gave no warning; only their v_identity (median 0.79, against 1.0 for the TRB contigs) gave them away. So split Cell Ranger's contigs by the annotations' chain column, and align each chain with its own model. The split keeps each contig's header as it is, so the ids still match the annotations: The first awk lists the contig_id of each annotation row of the chain; the second keeps those contigs of the FASTA. Add TRG and TRD to the loop for gamma-delta libraries, or loop over IGH IGK IGL for B cells. Contigs whose chain is Multi, or a chain no model covers, are left out. Each table carries cell_id, umi_count, consensus_count and c_call from the annotations. The tables have the same columns, so tcr.tsv is one table under one header, with each row's locus. AlignAIR does not pair chains. To pair them, join the rows of the two loci on cell_id; a cell with two chains of one locus keeps here the one with the most UMIs: Tables from several 10x runs need a sample_id before you merge them ( A sample id for every row), and cells are then keyed by sample_id and cell_id together.

title: Which column holds the read id
body: By default, the id column is the table's first column named sequence_id, contig_id, cell_id, id or name (any case); in Cell Ranger's table that is contig_id. Name another with --metadata-id-column: Ids are matched as the input file gives them, before a repeated id gets its _dup1 suffix, so both copies of a repeated read get its row. A read whose id is not in the table gets empty metadata columns. An id twice in the table is refused (ALIGNAIR_METADATA_ID_INVALID): choose a column whose values are unique.

title: Which columns are kept
body: By default, AlignAIR keeps those of these columns the table has: cell_id, barcode, sample_id, umi_count, umis, reads, duplicate_count, consensus_count, raw_clonotype_id, raw_consensus_id, chain, c_call, is_cell and high_confidence, plus the AIRR names above. --keep-columns chooses them yourself, by their names in the file (Cell Ranger's umis, not umi_count); a name the file does not have is an error.

title: A sample id for every row
body: The metadata is per read. To give every row of a sample's table the same sample_id, add the column after the run. Tables you merge need it: 10x barcodes repeat across runs, so AAACCTGAGAAACCAT-1 can be a cell of every sample. With one table per sample: Skip this when the metadata table already gave each read a sample_id (it is one of the columns kept by default).

title: Columns AlignAIR also writes: the meta_ prefix
body: Metadata never overwrites a value AlignAIR writes. A kept column whose name is one of AlignAIR's own columns is written as meta_<name>: keep Cell Ranger's productive and the table gets both AlignAIR's productive and Cell Ranger's meta_productive. c_call is the exception. AlignAIR does not call the constant region, so a metadata c_call (or Cell Ranger's c_gene) keeps its name and fills the column's empty cells.
